events.text: On the last evening of the conference, when the tea has gone cold, Cheon Uri stands up. They are the child of a god who faded long ago, and they ask it plainly: "If the Dao is already whole, who is it waiting for?" Ten thousand immortals turn to you. You find that you do not know.
events.arc: The Question on the Empty Stone

effects.log: You say it aloud. The terraces go so quiet that you hear the wind in the banners. Then, slowly, people begin to think.

choices.text: Give the best answer you have

effects.log: You answer well, and they applaud. Cheon Uri does not. They sit down and write your answer in a small book, and under it a question mark.

choices.text: Carve it into the stone of the first question

effects.log: You cut the words into the empty stone with one finger. From that night every conference begins by reading them.

events.text: Sixty years on, the question has two schools. Seo Dohwan of the Still Water teaches that the Dao waits for no one and the wise stop asking. Ryu Gaeun of the Open Hand teaches that it waits for each walker, and must be gone out to meet. Both climb to your seat on the same morning and ask you to judge.
events.arc: The Question on the Empty Stone

effects.log: You sit on Seo Dohwan's terrace. Half the conference follows you, and the other half goes down the steps singing.
You walk out with Ryu Gaeun. The Still Water does not argue. It only grows quieter, and deeper.

choices.text: Judge neither, and seat them side by side

effects.log: You put the two schools on one terrace with a single teapot between them. It is the loudest century the conference has known.

events.text: {sov_student} lectures on the question carved into your conference, and halfway through you understand that their answer is larger than yours. The terraces understand it too. Ten thousand heads turn, not to the lecturer, but to see what you will do.
events.arc: The Question on the Empty Stone

choices.text: Stand, and bow to your student

effects.log: You bow. {sov_student} stops mid-sentence, red to the ears, and then goes on, better than before.
You find the one flaw and name it. You are right. {sov_student} thanks you, and never lectures on the question again.

choices.text: Ask them to teach you, privately

effects.log: That night you sit at the feet of your own student and take notes. Neither of you tells anyone.

events.text: Do Yeonhwa, a clerk of the Heavenly Court, comes with ink on their sleeves and fear in their face. In the Book of Fates there is a page in no one's hand: the question from your stone, and under it, a blank line that no brush will mark. The Court wants the page removed.
events.arc: The Question on the Empty Stone

effects.log: The page is cut out with a silver knife. The Book closes more easily. You find you miss it.
You put your seal on the page. The Court is displeased, and the blank line stays blank.

choices.text: Take a brush and try to write the answer

ok.log: The brush marks the line, one word, and then the ink dries. The word is yours. You do not tell the clerk what it says.

fail.log: The brush slides off the line as if it were glass. Your hand aches for a year.

events.text: Seo Dohwan and Ryu Gaeun, who shared your teapot for a century, come together to tell you they have found the same thing from opposite sides: that the question cannot be answered by one walker alone. They want to found a third terrace, for asking together.
events.arc: The Question on the Empty Stone

effects.log: The third terrace opens with no lecturer at all, only circles of immortals talking. It is never empty again.

choices.text: Ask them to wait until you understand it

effects.log: They wait, politely. While they wait, the two schools drift apart again.

events.text: The two schools no longer share a staircase. The Still Water has closed its terrace to all but the silent; the Open Hand has gone down below the clouds to teach mortals the question in markets. Each sends you a letter asking you to call the other back.
events.arc: The Question on the Empty Stone

effects.log: Ryu Gaeun comes back up the steps with three thousand mortal questions in a sack. The Still Water is not pleased.
You sit at Seo Dohwan's gate until it opens. It takes nine years, and neither of you says a word.
You answer both letters with the same sentence: "The question went both ways too." They are both furious, and both keep it.

events.text: You dream that you sit on the empty stone and a voice asks Cheon Uri's question in your own voice. When you open your mouth to answer, you see the whole conference below you, every immortal you have ever taught, each holding one piece of something.
events.arc: The Question on the Empty Stone

choices.text: Try to gather the pieces in the dream

ok.log: For one breath you hold them all. You wake with an understanding you cannot put into words, and do not try.

fail.log: The pieces slip through your fingers like rain. You wake knowing only that they exist.

choices.text: Leave the pieces where they are

effects.log: You let each of them keep their piece. In the morning you teach more gently.

events.text: The one who surpassed you on the question has founded a conference of their own on the far side of heaven, on the same cycle as yours. Half your immortals now go there. They send you, every time, a seat at the front and a cup of the tea you taught them to make.
events.arc: The Question on the Empty Stone

choices.text: Go, and sit in the front row

effects.log: You attend your student's conference as a guest. It is the best lecture you have heard in an age.

choices.text: Move your own cycle so they never clash

effects.log: You change your calendar for your student. The immortals of heaven now have twice as many conferences.

choices.text: Hold yours on the very same day

effects.log: Heaven must choose. It chooses both, badly, and spends a century arguing about it.

events.text: The one you corrected before the whole conference has not lectured since. They come to you now, older, and say the flaw you named was real, and that they have spent the centuries since removing it. "Shall I lecture on the question again?" they ask. "Or was once enough?"
events.arc: The Question on the Empty Stone

choices.text: "Lecture. I will sit in the back row."

effects.log: They lecture. The flaw is gone, and so is something you did not know you had taken from them. It comes back.
They nod, and go. You were right, and the conference is smaller for it.

events.text: Cheon Uri climbs the terraces once more, very old for one of heaven, with the small book in which they wrote every answer anyone has ever given them. It is full. They open it to the first page, and ask if you have an answer now.
events.arc: The Question on the Empty Stone

effects.log: Cheon Uri laughs until they have to sit down. "Good," they say. "Neither have I. We are still walking."

choices.text: Tell them the word you wrote in the Book of Fates

effects.log: You whisper it. Cheon Uri writes it on the last line of the book, and closes it, and weeps a little.
Cheon Uri reads you the whole book, every answer, all night. At dawn you realise the book is the answer, or the nearest thing.

events.text: The conference opens and nobody speaks. Every immortal on every terrace has come only to sit with the carved question, and the silence spreads from terrace to terrace until even the heralds lower their banners. It lasts a year. The Court asks if you are ill.
events.arc: The Question on the Empty Stone

choices.text: Sit in the silence with them

effects.log: You sit for the whole year. When the first word is finally spoken, it is a child laughing, and the conference begins again.
You lecture into the silence. They listen, grateful, and something that was about to happen does not.
The founder of the Still Water arrives, looks at the terraces, and says, "At last." They sit down beside you.

events.text: You are old enough now that the heralds begin to ask who will keep the stone when you are gone. The question cannot be given away, but someone must read it aloud at the opening of every conference. Everyone on the terraces is careful not to look as if they want it.
events.arc: The Question on the Empty Stone

choices.text: Give it to Cheon Uri, who asked it

effects.log: Cheon Uri refuses three times and accepts the fourth. Their hands shake as they read the words aloud.

choices.text: Give it to the one who surpassed you

effects.log: You put the reading into the hands of the student who outgrew you. They read it better than you ever did.

choices.text: Give it to the youngest immortal present

effects.log: A child of the youngest school reads it, stumbling. The old immortals weep openly.

events.text: Your last conference as its host. The new keeper reads Cheon Uri's question from the stone, and then, by custom, turns to you for the answer, and the terraces wait, as they waited the first night. This time you know what to say.
events.arc: The Question on the Empty Stone

effects.log: You say it as you said it the first night. The whole of heaven answers you with one breath, and the conference goes on without you.
You point at them all. Ten thousand immortals understand at once that they are who the Dao was waiting for. Nobody can say it. Everybody knows.
You stand, bow to the stone, and walk down the stairs. The silence behind you is the best lecture you have ever given.

events.text: Cheon Uri asks to see you alone. The god who made them faded when nobody prayed any longer; there is no temple, no statue, only Cheon Uri, who remembers. They ask whether a god who is forgotten is gone, or only waiting.

choices.text: "Gone. You are what is left, and it is enough."

effects.log: Cheon Uri nods for a long time. Then they ask for a cup of tea, and drink it, and are steadier.
You promise to look. Cheon Uri looks at you as if you had handed them a lamp.

events.text: Your search takes you to the lowest shelf of the Silent Hall, where forgotten gods are filed by the dust they left. A keeper of the Hall finds the name of Cheon Uri's parent, and beside it, faintly, a single living prayer from somewhere below the clouds.

effects.log: An old mortal below, in a hill-town, still lights one stick of incense a year to a god they cannot name. You tell Cheon Uri.

choices.text: Bring the name to Cheon Uri and stop there

effects.log: Cheon Uri holds the name like a stone from home. It is enough. They do not ask for more.

events.text: Cheon Uri has gone below the clouds to the hill-town of the last prayer. They send you word: the old mortal is gone, but their grandchild lit the incense this year without knowing why, and the faded god stirred, a little, like a sleeper turning over.

choices.text: Send them faith to help it wake

effects.log: You send down a share of your own worship. Cheon Uri writes back one line: "It knows my name."

choices.text: Tell them some things should sleep

effects.log: Cheon Uri comes back up the clouds without waking it, and seems lighter for having chosen.

events.text: Cheon Uri has kept writing. The small book in which they put your answer under a question mark is now three books, and they bring all three, asking you to read what every god of heaven said when Cheon Uri asked them the same question.

effects.log: It takes you a season. Mujin of the Thousand Banners answered with a war; Saengmo, Mother of Seeds, with a seed. None of them is wrong.
You read your own answer again. It is clever. It is very small. You keep it in your sleeve for a century.

events.text: Someone has stolen Cheon Uri's books. The conference is in uproar: a dozen gods are named in them, and some of their answers were not meant for other gods to read. Cheon Uri sits on the steps with empty hands.

ok.log: A junior clerk of the Court, who wanted to know what the gods really think. You take the books back and let the clerk go, ashamed.

fail.log: The books are never found. Cheon Uri starts again, from the first page, in a new book.

choices.text: Help them start a new book

effects.log: You write the first answer of the new book yourself. It is shorter than your old one, and better.

events.text: Cheon Uri asks your permission to read the books aloud at the conference, every answer of every god, without names. The gods who answered are nervous. The immortals are thrilled.

effects.log: The reading takes nine days. On the tenth, three gods come to Cheon Uri privately to change their answers.

choices.text: Allow it, but only the gods who consent

effects.log: Half consent. The reading is shorter, and kinder, and nobody leaves angry.

events.text: You find Cheon Uri on the lowest terrace teaching three new immortals to make the conference tea the way you make it: leaves first, then the water a little too hot, then wait longer than seems right. They do not see you. They are better at explaining it than you are.

effects.log: You go back up the steps without a word. The tea that night is perfect.
Cheon Uri laughs and pours it out and begins again. "Even the tea has a teacher," they say.

events.text: Yeon Seorin, who stood nine thousand years at one gate of the Dao, comes back to your terraces with news: the gate opened. Not for any teaching. It opened one morning while they were sweeping in front of it. They are frightened to walk through alone.
events.arc: The Gate of Nine Thousand Years

effects.log: You step through the gate together. On the other side is a small garden, and Yeon Seorin sits down in it and cries for a day.
Yeon Seorin goes through alone. You wait a month. They come back changed, and grateful you let them go alone.
They blink. "Leaves," they say. "Every day, for nine thousand years." You both begin to laugh.

events.text: Yeon Seorin now stands at a second gate, and every immortal on the terraces has heard of it. Young immortals line up behind them to stand at gates of their own, and a whole terrace of your conference has become a field of waiting.
events.arc: The Gate of Nine Thousand Years

effects.log: You hand out brooms. The Field of Gates becomes the tidiest terrace in heaven, and three gates open in a century.

choices.text: Tell the young ones to find their own way

effects.log: Most leave. A few stay, and those few are the ones who would have stayed anyway.

events.text: Yeon Seorin has opened their last gate and found it opens onto your conference. They laugh about it for a week. Then they ask you, seriously, for a terrace of their own, to teach patience to immortals who have forgotten it.
events.arc: The Gate of Nine Thousand Years

choices.text: Give them the Field of Gates

effects.log: The patient teacher has a terrace now. Their lectures start late and end when they end.

choices.text: Ask them to teach you first

effects.log: You stand at a gate under Yeon Seorin's eye for thirty years. It does not open. You learn a great deal.

events.text: A sect below the clouds has written to the conference. Its founder was Yeon Seorin, nine thousand years ago, and its disciples worship them now as a distant immortal they will never meet. They have asked, timidly, whether the founder still lives.
events.arc: The Sect That Forgot Yeon Seorin

effects.log: Yeon Seorin reads the letter four times. "They kept the name," they say, and cannot say anything else.
You write that their founder is alive, patient and well. The whole sect holds a festival below.

events.text: Yeon Seorin wants to go down to the sect they founded, but is afraid the disciples will be disappointed by a teacher who stood at a gate for most of history. They ask you to come with them, as a god, so that someone in the room is impressive.
events.arc: The Sect That Forgot Yeon Seorin

effects.log: You arrive in light. The sect bows to you, and then, when Yeon Seorin speaks, forgets you completely.

choices.text: Send them alone, with your seal

effects.log: Yeon Seorin goes alone, and is not disappointing in the least.

events.text: The sect of Yeon Seorin sends its best disciple up the clouds to your conference: a nervous young cultivator called Yeon Dari, who took their founder's family name out of reverence. They have brought a broom.
events.arc: The Sect That Forgot Yeon Seorin

choices.text: Seat them at the Field of Gates

effects.log: Yeon Dari sweeps beside their founder. The two of them look absurdly alike.

ok.log: They answer like someone who has been taught by a gate. You are delighted.

fail.log: They freeze, and sweep instead of answering. You find that is also an answer.

events.text: Gwak Taeseong has stopped asking why you gave the sword back. Now they want to know what it would have been worth if you had not. They challenge you, before the conference, to a duel of understanding: no blows, only one question each.
events.arc: The Duel on the Upper Terrace

effects.log: You agree. The terraces fill as they have not filled since the first conference.
Gwak Taeseong drinks the tea, and calls you a coward, and drinks a second cup.

events.text: The duel of questions. Gwak Taeseong asks first: "What is a sword for, when nobody is left to fight?" The terraces hold their breath.
events.arc: The Duel on the Upper Terrace

ok.log: "For cutting bread," you say. Gwak Taeseong laughs so hard they lose the duel.

fail.log: Your answer is good, and wrong for them. Gwak Taeseong wins the round and does not gloat.

choices.text: Ask them back: "Who are you fighting now?"

effects.log: The sword immortal is silent a long time. "Myself," they say, and lower their eyes. Nobody wins.

events.text: Gwak Taeseong brings you a sword of plain iron, the first they ever held, from a mortal smithy below the clouds. They want you to keep it. "I have been fighting you for centuries," they say. "I think I was fighting to be taught."
events.arc: The Duel on the Upper Terrace

effects.log: You take the iron sword and hang it over the conference gate. Gwak Taeseong takes a seat in the front row.
"Still yours," you say. Gwak Taeseong grins. "I knew you would," they say, and that is the end of the rivalry.

events.text: The sword terraces Gwak Taeseong runs have grown so fierce that the gods of the Will of Heaven come to watch. Mujin of the Thousand Banners, god of War, asks you to lend Gwak to train their banner-captains.

effects.log: Gwak Taeseong goes, grumbling. Mujin's captains come back humbler, and Mujin sends you a banner in thanks.
Gwak Taeseong refuses the god of War to their face. Mujin is so impressed they enrol a captain anyway.

events.text: One of Gwak Taeseong's students has cut through a pillar of the conference in a training bout. Not a mark: through. The pillar was older than heaven's Court. Gwak stands before you with the student, both of them pale.

choices.text: Praise the cut, then mend the pillar

effects.log: You mend the pillar and leave the line of the cut showing. Students come for centuries to touch it.

choices.text: Make them mend it by hand

effects.log: Teacher and student spend nine years on scaffolding. Gwak Taeseong says it was the best lesson of their life.

events.text: Gwak Taeseong asks to retire from the sword terraces. They have no more to teach the sword, they say, and would like to sit in the back of the conference and learn something they are bad at. They would like to learn music.

effects.log: You send for a flute-player of the Green Assembly. Gwak is terrible at it, and happier than in a thousand years.
You are not good at music either. The two of you play badly together on the high terrace, and the immortals pretend not to hear.

events.text: Gwak Taeseong is old now, older than any sword immortal has a right to be. They climb your terraces slowly, and sit on the steps, and ask one last question: "When I am gone, will the sword terraces remember why they began?"

effects.log: Gwak laughs, and coughs, and laughs. "Tell them that," they say. "Tell them it was rude."

choices.text: "They will, because I will tell them every year."

effects.log: You promise. Gwak Taeseong nods, satisfied, and goes to sit in the sun.

events.text: Gwak Taeseong does not come to the conference this cycle. A student brings you the iron sword and a note in a clumsy hand: they have gone down to the mortal smithy where it was forged, to live out their years beside the fire, and wish you a good lecture.

choices.text: Read the note at the opening

effects.log: You read it to ten thousand immortals. Every sword on the sword terraces is laid down for an hour.
You find Gwak hammering a horseshoe, badly, and smiling. You stay for supper.

events.text: Ha Jiwoo, the mortal-born star-fisher Gwak Taeseong brought you, has grown up. They still fish for stars, from the edge of the highest terrace, with a line of their own hair. Last night they caught one. It is very small and very angry.

effects.log: The star goes back to the sky, sulking. Cheonho, Who Hangs the Stars, sends you a note: "Thank you. Do not let that happen again."

choices.text: Let them keep it a night

effects.log: Ha Jiwoo talks to the star all night. In the morning they release it, and understand something about distance.

events.text: Cheonho, Who Hangs the Stars, god of the Sky, has come to the conference in person, which they never do, to see who has been fishing their sky. Ha Jiwoo stands up from the edge, line in hand, too surprised to bow.

effects.log: Cheonho looks Ha Jiwoo up and down, and then offers to teach them how a star is hung. Ha Jiwoo cannot speak.

choices.text: Let Ha Jiwoo speak for themself

effects.log: Ha Jiwoo apologises to the god of the Sky and then asks how deep the sky is. Cheonho stays a whole season answering.

events.text: Ha Jiwoo has hung their first star, small, low on the horizon of heaven, under Cheonho's eye. It is a little crooked. They ask you to come and look, and stand very straight beside it.

choices.text: Tell them it is crooked, and perfect

effects.log: Ha Jiwoo laughs with relief. The crooked star is still there, and immortals make wishes on it.
The crooked star is called Gwak's Interruption. Gwak pretends to be furious and visits it every year.

events.text: Ha Jiwoo asks leave to visit the mortal fishing-town below where they were born. Everyone they knew is long gone. They want to see if anybody there still fishes at night.

effects.log: You walk the harbour below in a fisher's coat. Children still fish there at night, and look up.

choices.text: Give them a season and your blessing

effects.log: Ha Jiwoo goes down alone, and writes every week.

events.text: Ha Jiwoo writes from the harbour below: a child there catches stars, too, only reflections in the water, but caught. They want to bring the child up the clouds when the child is grown, if you will allow a second star-fisher.

effects.log: Eighty years later a grey-haired mortal-born immortal climbs your terraces with a fishing line. Ha Jiwoo runs to meet them.

choices.text: Tell them to teach the child below

effects.log: Ha Jiwoo stays in the harbour for a lifetime, teaching. A school of star-fishers grows there.

events.text: Somebody has left a broom leaning against the stone of the first question. The terraces argue all morning about whether it is a joke, a lesson or an offering. Yeon Seorin walks past, sees it, and smiles, and keeps walking.

effects.log: The broom stays a century. Then somebody uses it, and that seems right too.
You sweep the stone in front of everyone. The arguing stops.

events.text: A letter arrives from Gwak Taeseong, who is not at this conference: "Somebody in your third row is going to ask a foolish question about the sword. Answer it kindly. It was mine, once." In the third row, someone is raising a hand.

effects.log: The question is foolish. You answer it as if it were not. The immortal who asked it goes very red, then very still.
The whole conference laughs, and the immortal asks anyway, braver for it.

events.text: Under the crooked star Ha Jiwoo hung, a young god of the Green Assembly has left a wish written on a leaf: that the conference would one day be held at night, so that the star could hear the lectures.

effects.log: You lecture under the crooked star. It seems, to everyone, a little brighter.

choices.text: Pin the leaf on the conference gate

effects.log: The leaf stays pinned for an age. Nobody agrees what it means.

events.text: Seo Dohwan, founder of the Still Water, has taken a vow not to speak for a hundred years, to prove their teaching. Their students now lecture for them by watching their face. The lectures are very short and rather good.
events.arc: The Vow of the Still Water

effects.log: You sit an afternoon before Seo Dohwan's silence. At the end you find you have been answered.
Seo Dohwan looks at you so patiently that you answer it yourself, out loud, and blush.

events.text: Halfway through the hundred years, a student of the Still Water has fallen ill of a deviation in their meditation. Only Seo Dohwan knows the cure, and to give it they must speak, and break the vow.
events.arc: The Vow of the Still Water

effects.log: You go into the student's mind and find the knot. Seo Dohwan keeps the vow, and bows to you to the ground.

choices.text: Tell Seo Dohwan the vow is a teaching, not a cage

effects.log: Seo Dohwan speaks one sentence, the cure. The student lives. The Still Water learns more from that sentence than from fifty years of silence.

events.text: The hundred years end. The whole conference gathers to hear the first words of Seo Dohwan in a century. They stand up on the Still Water terrace, look over ten thousand faces, and say: "Is there any tea?"
events.arc: The Vow of the Still Water

effects.log: You pour. The conference laughs for an hour, and the Still Water gains a thousand students.
Your laugh starts it. Seo Dohwan looks offended, then delighted. It is the first joke of the Still Water.

events.text: Baekun the Pale Ferryman, god of Death in the Silent Hall, has offered the Still Water a home: a pool in their hall where nothing ever moves. Seo Dohwan is tempted. It would mean leaving your conference.
events.arc: Seo Dohwan and the Silent Hall

choices.text: Tell them to go, with your blessing

effects.log: Seo Dohwan goes to the still pool. The Silent Hall grows wiser, and your terraces quieter.
Seo Dohwan stays, and the Ferryman takes it graciously, and comes to your next conference in a grey hood.

choices.text: Propose a terrace in both places

effects.log: The Still Water keeps a seat at your conference and a pool in the Silent Hall. Its students travel between them in silence.

events.text: A god of the Silent Hall brings you a message from Seo Dohwan, written on a smooth stone: the still pool shows the faces of everyone who ever asked the question on your stone. They have counted a hundred thousand, and they ask you to come and see your own.
events.arc: Seo Dohwan and the Silent Hall

effects.log: In the still pool your face is the first one, young and lost. You did not know you had looked like that.
Seo Dohwan understands. Some faces are not to be looked at.

events.text: The god Baekun the Pale Ferryman comes to you in a grey hood. Seo Dohwan has sat beside the still pool so long that the Ferryman is no longer sure they are alive. "I would like to row them across," the god says, "or wake them. You are their teacher. Choose."
events.arc: Seo Dohwan and the Silent Hall

ok.log: You call Seo Dohwan's name across a hundred years of stillness. They open their eyes, and ask, again, for tea.

fail.log: They do not wake. The Ferryman waits with you a year, and then they stir on their own.

effects.log: You let them sit. The Ferryman nods, and leaves the oar beside the pool.

events.text: Ryu Gaeun of the Open Hand has gone below the clouds and set up a stall in a mortal market, with a sign: ONE QUESTION, ANSWERED FREE. The queue is enormous. A great many of the questions are about rent.
events.arc: The Open Hand at a Mortal Stall

choices.text: Send them a helper from the conference

effects.log: A young immortal is sent down to help answer about rent. They come back two centuries later the most practical teacher in heaven.

choices.text: Go and stand in the queue yourself

effects.log: You wait your turn below, in plain clothes. When you reach the stall Ryu Gaeun looks up, and laughs, and answers you.

events.text: The Heavenly Court has sent a warrant to the conference: an immortal of the Open Hand is teaching cultivation to mortals without leave, and the Court calls it meddling. The warrant names Ryu Gaeun.
events.arc: The Open Hand at a Mortal Stall

choices.text: Speak for them before the Court

effects.log: You argue for a day. The Court settles on a licence, and the Open Hand gets the first one ever written.

choices.text: Tell Ryu Gaeun to come home for a while

effects.log: Ryu Gaeun comes home angry, and teaches the angriest lectures of the age.

choices.text: Hide the stall from the Court's eyes

ok.log: The Court's clerks walk past it for a century.

fail.log: The clerks find it. You are fined in merit and in face.

events.text: A mortal who once asked Ryu Gaeun about rent below has become a cultivator, and then an immortal, and now climbs to your terraces with their first real question. Ryu Gaeun watches from the side, so proud they cannot sit still.
events.arc: The Open Hand at a Mortal Stall

effects.log: Ryu Gaeun answers. It is the best answer of the conference. It is also about rent, in a way.

choices.text: Answer it yourself, and give Ryu the credit

effects.log: You answer, and say where you learned it. Ryu Gaeun goes red to the ears.

events.text: Ryu Gaeun has given away so much of their cultivation teaching below that their own realm has begun to slip. Their students notice first. Ryu notices last, and laughs about it, and keeps giving.
events.arc: The Hand That Would Not Close

choices.text: Give them some of your own enlightenment

effects.log: You pass a measure of your understanding into Ryu Gaeun's open hand. They hold it, and for once do not give it away.

choices.text: Tell them to close the hand a while

effects.log: Ryu Gaeun sulks for a decade, and rests, and their realm steadies. They admit you were right, sulkily.

events.text: Ryu Gaeun's students have founded a hundred small Open Hand schools below the clouds. Some teach well. One, in a mortal river-town, has begun to take payment for the question, and calls itself the only true hand.
events.arc: The Hand That Would Not Close

choices.text: Send Ryu to set it right

effects.log: Ryu Gaeun closes the false school with one lecture, given free, in its own courtyard.
The river-town stops paying within a generation. Ryu Gaeun is disappointed it took so long.

events.text: Ryu Gaeun climbs to you with empty hands, palms up, as their school has always shown them. "I have given away everything," they say. "Even the question. I don't remember what it was." They are smiling, and frightened.
events.arc: The Hand That Would Not Close

choices.text: Read it to them from the stone

effects.log: You read it aloud. Ryu Gaeun listens like someone hearing a song they once knew. "Oh," they say. "Yes."
Ryu Gaeun stares at you a long while, and then sits down in the sun and does not get up for a year.

events.text: Mok Hyeran, an archivist immortal with ink-stained fingers, asks leave to keep a Record of Questions: every question ever asked at your conference, with no answers, only who asked and when. "Answers go stale," they say. "Questions keep."

choices.text: Grant it, and give them a hall

effects.log: Mok Hyeran moves into a hall of empty shelves and begins. The first entry is yours.

choices.text: Grant it, but with the answers too

effects.log: Mok Hyeran agrees, unhappily. The Record is twice as long and half as read.

events.text: The Record of Questions has filled ninety shelves. Mok Hyeran has found that one question has been asked at every conference, in different words, by a different immortal each time, and nobody noticed. They want to know if you did.

effects.log: Mok Hyeran nods. "That is why I write it down," they say, and shows you all the forms of it.
They read it to you. It is about loneliness. You sit with that for a long time.

events.text: A god of the Will of Heaven wants the Record of Questions burned. Some of the questions in it, they say, are about the Heavenly Court, and should never have been asked aloud, let alone written down.

effects.log: You put the Record under your own seal. The god is offended for a thousand years, and the Record is read more than ever.

choices.text: Let Mok Hyeran hide the worst shelves

effects.log: Mok Hyeran hides nine shelves where only an archivist would look. The god goes away satisfied.

choices.text: Ask the god what question frightens them

ok.log: They tell you, in a whisper. Mok Hyeran writes it in the Record, with the god's name, at the god's own wish.

fail.log: The god will not say. They leave, and the Record is safe, for now.

events.text: Mok Hyeran is old, and the Record has grown to a building of its own. They ask who will keep it when they are gone, and say, firmly, that it should not be anyone who likes answers.

choices.text: Find them an apprentice who only asks

effects.log: You find a quiet immortal who has never answered a question in their life. Mok Hyeran approves on sight.
You promise to keep the Record. Mok Hyeran laughs. "You like answers," they say, "but you are trying."

events.text: Mok Hyeran has found a gap in the Record. At the conference three hundred years ago, one question was asked and never written down. They have asked every immortal who was there. Nobody remembers it.

choices.text: Search your own memory for it

ok.log: You find it, small and sharp: a child asked if gods are ever afraid. You answered no. You were lying.

fail.log: It is gone. Some questions leave without a trace.

choices.text: Leave the gap in the Record

effects.log: Mok Hyeran draws a small empty box in the Record, and labels it: Asked.

events.text: Mok Hyeran has written the forgotten question back into the Record: whether gods are ever afraid. Beside it, by custom, a space for the asker's name. The child who asked is now an immortal, and comes to read it.

choices.text: Tell them the true answer now

effects.log: "Yes," you say. "That day, too." The immortal who was a child nods, as if they always knew.
"Yes," they say. "That is why we asked." Mok Hyeran writes that down too.

events.text: Seo Dohwan of the Still Water and Ryu Gaeun of the Open Hand reach for the last cup of tea on the high terrace at the same moment. Ten thousand immortals stop. The two founders look at the cup, and then at each other, and then at you.

effects.log: You drink it. Both founders laugh. The schools talk about it as a teaching for centuries.
Two half cups. Both schools claim this as their teaching.
Neither yields. The tea goes cold. That is also a teaching.

events.text: You find Mok Hyeran asleep across the open Record of Questions, ink on one cheek, with the lamp nearly out. The page under their hand is the very first one, the one with your question on it.

effects.log: You trim it and go. In the morning the page is wet with a little spilled tea, and Mok Hyeran pretends it was always so.
Your old question was clumsier than you remembered. You are glad it was asked.

events.text: A student of the Still Water and a student of the Open Hand ask you to marry them at the conference, before both schools. Seo Dohwan and Ryu Gaeun, who have not agreed on anything in a century, both say it is a terrible idea.

effects.log: You marry them on the stone of the first question. The two founders sit side by side and both weep.

choices.text: Tell them to wait until the founders agree

effects.log: They wait. The founders, cornered, agree within the year.

events.text: {sov_student} has asked to give a lecture of their own at the next conference. They have been practising it for twenty years in an empty courtyard, to a tree. They are so nervous that their qi makes the tea boil in the cup.
events.arc: The First Lecture of a Student

effects.log: You sit where they can see you. {sov_student} looks at you once, breathes, and begins.
{sov_student} cannot find you, and so gives the lecture to the whole conference instead. It is better that way.

choices.text: Go and talk to the tree

effects.log: The tree has heard the lecture two thousand times. It is, in its slow way, quite proud.

events.text: The lecture of {sov_student} went well, and now three hundred immortals want to study with them, not with you. They come to you, embarrassed, to ask whether they should send them back to your terrace.
events.arc: The First Lecture of a Student

effects.log: {sov_student} takes their first students. You hear them use your words, and some words that are entirely their own.
You take the twelve worst-behaved. {sov_student} is very grateful, and you are very busy.

events.text: One of the first students of {sov_student} has made a breakthrough and comes running to tell you, not their own teacher. {sov_student} stands behind them in the doorway, smiling, and a little hurt.
events.arc: The First Lecture of a Student

choices.text: Send the student back to their teacher

effects.log: "Tell {sov_student} first," you say. The student runs back. You hear them shout it down the hall.
You open the good tea for the three of you. Nobody is hurt by the end of the pot.

events.text: {sov_student} and {sov_student_b} have quarrelled on the great stair of the conference over which of them understood your last lecture. They have both written ten thousand words on it. Each asks you to read theirs first.

effects.log: You read both at once, a page of each. They are describing the same thing from either end.

choices.text: Read neither, and give a new lecture

effects.log: You lecture on the same thing again, worse. Both students, united, correct you.
{sov_student_b} wrote fewer words. They are insufferable for a decade.

events.text: {sov_student_b} has left the conference for a remote crag of the Throne of Storms, and writes that they will not come back while {sov_student} sits in the front row. {sov_student} pretends not to care, very badly.

effects.log: You sit with {sov_student_b} through three thunderstorms. On the fourth they agree to come back to the second row.
{sov_student} goes, grumbling. They come back a month later together, and refuse to say what was said.

events.text: {sov_student} and {sov_student_b} have written a book together on your teaching. It disagrees with you in three places. They hand it to you together, and stand very close, as if for protection.

choices.text: Read it, and agree in two places

effects.log: You agree with two. On the third you argue all night, the three of you, and it is the best night of the century.
You sign the book. They are disappointed: they wanted the argument.

events.text: {sov_strival}, once your student, has announced a Grand Dao Conference of their own, on the far side of heaven, on the very years of yours. The heralds of both conferences pass each other on the golden roads and pretend not to see.

choices.text: Send a herald to wish them well

effects.log: Your herald arrives with a gift of your best tea. {sov_strival} sends it back unopened, and then, a week later, asks for more.
You change nothing. Half the immortals go to {sov_strival}. The half who stay are the ones you most wanted.
You sit in the back row of your rival's conference. They teach well. They teach some things you never taught.

events.text: At the rival conference {sov_strival} has said aloud that your teaching on the question is a comfortable lie. Your students are furious. A delegation of them asks leave to go and argue.

effects.log: They go, and lose, and come home with better questions than they left with.
You stand up in your rival's conference and ask one question. {sov_strival} answers it. It is a good answer. You bow and sit down.
Your students obey, and resent it. It takes a century for the conference to feel warm again.

events.text: {sov_strival} has fallen ill of a deviation in a sealed retreat, and their students do not know what to do. One of them comes to your conference gate in tears and asks, against their teacher's orders, for you.

effects.log: You break the seal and sit with {sov_strival} for nine days. When they wake, the first thing they do is argue with you.

ok.log: Your notes, in your own hand, reach the retreat. {sov_strival} heals by them, and keeps the notes forever.

fail.log: The notes arrive late. {sov_strival} recovers, slowly and alone.

events.text: Nine of your best students have gone over to {sov_strival}'s conference in one season. They left a letter: you teach how to ask, and they want to learn how to win.

choices.text: Let them go with your blessing

effects.log: You send them their notes and a letter of thanks. Two come back within a century, gently.

choices.text: Answer the letter with a lecture on winning

effects.log: You lecture on winning, better than they expected. Four come back. You are not proud of how.

events.text: One of the students who went over to {sov_strival} has come back, alone, and sits outside your gate. They say the rival teaches brilliantly, and that they were lonely there, and they do not know which of those matters more.

choices.text: Take them back without a word

effects.log: They take their old seat. Within a decade nobody remembers they ever left.

choices.text: Send them back with a question for the rival

effects.log: They carry your question back. {sov_strival} answers it in a lecture and sends you a copy, unsigned.

events.text: {sov_strival} has sent you a student of their own: a young immortal who asked them a question they could not answer. The note says only, in your old student's hand: "This one is yours."

effects.log: You answer it. It takes you a year. You write the answer to {sov_strival}, too.

choices.text: Send the student back: "Then it is yours to find."

effects.log: The student goes back. {sov_strival} finds the answer, after all, and is better for it.

events.text: After centuries of rival conferences, {sov_strival} climbs your stairs, alone, with no herald. They stand on the top step and do not come in. "I have taught everything I know," they say. "I would like to learn something."

effects.log: You seat {sov_strival} in the front row of your conference. Neither of you mentions the centuries.

choices.text: Ask them to give the lecture

effects.log: {sov_strival} lectures on your terrace. Both conferences, for once, are in one place.

choices.text: Tell them you would like to learn too

effects.log: You go and sit beside them on the top step. The conference starts without either of you.

events.text: {sov_strival} has merged their conference into yours, on one condition: that the rival terrace stays, with its own banner, and that every lecture on yours may be argued with on theirs. Your heralds are aghast.

effects.log: The Grand Dao Conference has a terrace of argument now. It is the most crowded in heaven.

choices.text: Ask that it argue with the rival too

effects.log: {sov_strival} laughs for the first time in your hearing in a thousand years, and agrees.

events.text: {sov_heir}, whom you named heir of your Dao, cannot sleep. Every immortal on the terraces now watches them for flaws. They come to you at night and ask whether you can take the name back and give it to someone stronger.

choices.text: "No. I chose you as you are."

effects.log: {sov_heir} goes back to bed, and, for the first time since the naming, sleeps.

choices.text: "Yes, if you ask me again in a year."

effects.log: They do not ask again. A year is long enough to learn to carry something.

events.text: A god of the Heavenly Court has questioned whether {sov_heir} is fit to be heir to a Supreme God's Dao, and wants it tested before the Court. {sov_heir} says they will go, if you think they should.

choices.text: Let them face the test alone

effects.log: {sov_heir} passes the Court's test without you in the room. The god who asked for it bows to them.

choices.text: Go and stand at their back

effects.log: You stand behind them through the whole test. They pass, and say afterwards that they could feel you there.
The Court yields to you. {sov_heir} is relieved, and a little sorry not to have been tested.

events.text: {sov_heir} has begun to teach the way you taught, gesture for gesture, even the way you lift the tea. Your oldest students find it charming. Mok Hyeran, keeper of the Record, finds it worrying, and says so.

choices.text: Tell {sov_heir} to find their own way

effects.log: {sov_heir} drops the gestures, and for a while teaches badly, and then teaches in a way nobody has seen before.

choices.text: Let them copy until they outgrow it

effects.log: They copy for two centuries. Then one day they lift the tea with the other hand, and you smile.

events.text: {sov_heir} has written to you from a far domain where they now teach: they have found a question you never asked, and do not know if they are allowed to ask it in your name.

effects.log: {sov_heir} asks it in their own name. It becomes the question of the next age.

choices.text: "Ask it in mine, and add yours."

effects.log: Two names stand under the new question. It reads better that way.

events.text: {sov_heir} asks for one last lesson before taking the conference: anything at all, they say, so long as it is the last one, so that they will know which one it was.

choices.text: Teach them to make the tea

effects.log: You teach them the conference tea, leaves first, water too hot, wait too long. {sov_heir} laughs and then understands, and does not laugh.

choices.text: Refuse: there is no last lesson

effects.log: {sov_heir} is angry, then very still. "Then I will never stop learning from you," they say. That was the lesson.

events.text: {sov_heir} hosts their first conference, and you sit in the back row, unannounced. On the stone of the first question they have left the old words, and under them, very small, a new line in their own hand.

choices.text: Go and read the new line

effects.log: It says: "My teacher did not know either." You sit down on the step and laugh until the heralds come to see.
You leave it for another century. It is good to have something still to read.

events.text: {sov_student} has kept every note you ever left in the margins of their work, and has bound them into a book for your birthday. Reading it, you find you have written the word "again" four hundred times.

effects.log: {sov_student} frames that page. They say it was the hardest lesson of all.
{sov_student} laughs, and does it again.

events.text: {sov_student_b} dreams the same dream three nights running: your conference empty, the tea warm, and nobody at all on the stone. They ask you if it is a prophecy, or a fear, or a hope.

choices.text: "A hope. One day it will not need me."

effects.log: {sov_student_b} goes away comforted, and a little unsettled.
Mongsa the Sleeper, god of Dreams, says only: "Yes." You both decide that is enough.

events.text: A packet of tea arrives with no letter, but you know the leaves: the ones you taught {sov_strival} to choose a thousand years ago, picked, dried and folded exactly as you showed them.

effects.log: It is very good tea. You drink it slowly, and think about your old student.
The whole conference drinks your rival's tea. Nobody but you knows.

events.text: {sov_heir} has given a wrong answer at the conference, before ten thousand immortals, and not noticed. You have noticed. So has the third row, which is looking at you.

choices.text: Say nothing until they are alone

effects.log: That night you show them. {sov_heir} corrects it themselves at the next session, and the third row nods.

choices.text: Correct it gently on the spot

effects.log: The mistake is mended in a breath. {sov_heir} thanks you, and does not sleep that night.

events.text: This is far from the first conference you have hosted, and the oldest immortals have begun to keep a seating plan of their own on the terraces: the same faces in the same places, century after century, like stars that only rise for you.

effects.log: The old faces grumble for a whole conference and talk to new people for the first time in an age.
You walk the terraces and name them all. It takes eleven days. Several old immortals weep.

events.text: Bang Soyul has made the tea for your conference since the third cycle, and has never once attended a lecture. They say they learn more from what is left in the cups. This year they ask for one thing: to give a lecture, on tea.

effects.log: Bang Soyul lectures on tea for an hour. Ten thousand immortals go home and make it differently.

choices.text: Ask them what the cups say

effects.log: Bang Soyul tells you which terrace drank fast, which forgot, which wept. You learn more than from any report.

events.text: Bang Soyul has found a leaf in the conference tea that should not be there: a leaf from the Harvest domain, grown by Pungnyeon of the Golden Field, that makes whoever drinks it agree with whoever speaks next. Someone has been seeding it.

ok.log: An ambitious young god who wanted the conference to agree with their lecture. You let the conference decide what to do with them. It laughs.

fail.log: The seeder is never found. Bang Soyul picks every leaf by hand for a century.

choices.text: Ask Pungnyeon to stop growing it

effects.log: The god of the Harvest is mortified, and uproots every bush of it in heaven. They come to the next conference to apologise in person.

events.text: Bang Soyul is retiring, and wants to pass the kettle on. They have three apprentices: one who is fast, one who is careful, and one who keeps forgetting the tea and listening to the lectures.

effects.log: The careful apprentice makes the tea for a thousand years and never once makes it badly.
The tea is late for a century. Then it is the best tea heaven has ever drunk, because the brewer knows what it is for.
They choose the fast one, and wink at you. The fast one turns out to be the most patient of all.

events.text: Bang Soyul tells you that one god has come to every conference for three hundred years and never touched the tea. They sit on the edge of the lowest terrace in a plain robe. Bang Soyul thinks it is an insult. You are not sure.
events.arc: The Guest Who Would Not Drink

choices.text: Take the cup to them yourself

effects.log: You bring the cup down. The god takes it, and holds it, and does not drink. "Not yet," they say.

choices.text: Ask Bang Soyul to make them something else

effects.log: Bang Soyul brews plain hot water. The god drinks it at once, and nods to Bang Soyul with great respect.

events.text: The god on the lowest terrace has finally drunk the conference tea. They put the cup down and tell you who they are: a god of a domain that no longer exists, sworn not to drink until something in heaven was worth staying for.
events.arc: The Guest Who Would Not Drink

effects.log: "Rain on the first night of spring," they say. You offer them a seat on the high terrace, and they take it.
They drink the second one slowly. They come every cycle after that, and drink every time.

events.text: Saengmo, Mother of Seeds, god of Life in the Green Assembly, has sent you a student: a sapling-spirit called Namu, potted in a bowl of their own soil. They do not speak. Saengmo's note says they will, once they have heard enough.

choices.text: Set them by the stone of the first question

effects.log: Namu stands in the sun by the stone. The immortals start lecturing to them by accident.

choices.text: Plant them in the earth of the terrace

effects.log: Namu sinks roots into your conference. Saengmo is pleased: you have accepted the student for life.

events.text: Namu has spoken their first word, at the conference, in the middle of a lecture on the Dao of Time. The word is "Wait." The lecturer stops. Nobody knows who Namu was talking to.

effects.log: You wait. The whole conference waits. After an hour a leaf falls from Namu, and the lecturer finishes, better.
"Rain," Namu says, the second word. It rains that afternoon for the first time in a hundred years on your terraces.

events.text: Namu has grown into a young tree and is no longer content to stand still. Through Saengmo they ask to be uprooted and carried around the conference to every terrace, so that they can hear all the schools.

effects.log: A Supreme God carries a potted tree from terrace to terrace for a whole conference. Nobody laughs. Mostly.
Namu rides a little cart from lecture to lecture, rustling at the good parts.

events.text: Namu has flowered. In every flower there is a word they heard at one of your conferences. Saengmo comes to see, and tells you Namu wishes to go home now, to the Green Assembly, and teach the forest what the gods talk about.

choices.text: Let them go, with a terrace stone

effects.log: Namu goes home with a stone from your terrace at their roots. The forest of the Green Assembly begins to rustle in sentences.
Namu gives you a seed. You plant it by the stone of the first question. It does not come up for a thousand years.

events.text: The seed Namu gave you has come up, after a thousand years, beside the stone of the first question. It is a thin green shoot, and already it has one word written on its single leaf. Nobody can read the script.

effects.log: The Mother of Seeds reads it and laughs: it is Namu's word for you. It means, roughly, the one who waits.
You leave the shoot alone. It grows a second leaf, and a third, each with a word you cannot read.

events.text: The second Namu is a sapling now, and every immortal who passes the stone touches its leaves for luck. Saengmo writes from the Green Assembly that the first Namu, far away, rustles whenever it happens.

effects.log: You lecture under the second Namu. Somewhere in the Green Assembly the forest listens.

choices.text: Build it a fence against the luck-seekers

effects.log: The second Namu grows a thicker trunk in peace. The first Namu, they say, was sorry about the fence.

events.text: Han Ilseong, an old god of the Silent Hall, has attended every one of your conferences and never said a word. They sit in the same place, at the same angle, and leave before the last lecture. This year, they leave you a folded paper.

effects.log: The paper is blank. Folded inside it is a pressed flower from the Silent Hall, where nothing grows.
You keep the paper folded for a century. When you finally open it, it is blank, and you understand.

events.text: Han Ilseong has not come this cycle. The place where they sit is empty, and every immortal on that terrace keeps a little distance from it, as if it were still taken.

choices.text: Go to the Silent Hall to find them

effects.log: You find Han Ilseong in the Hall, sitting at the same angle. They nod to you, and that is all. It is a great deal.
Their seat stays empty through the whole conference. Next cycle they are back in it, and the terrace relaxes.

events.text: At the very end of a conference, after every other immortal has gone, Han Ilseong stands, walks to the stone of the first question, and for the first time in your hearing speaks: "Thank you." Then they go home.

effects.log: You say it back to an empty terrace. You hope it carries to the Silent Hall. It does.

choices.text: Write it in the Record of Questions

effects.log: Mok Hyeran's Record has its first entry that is not a question. Nobody objects.

events.text: A messenger of the Silent Hall brings word that Han Ilseong is fading: their worshippers below are gone, and their name is nearly forgotten. They have asked for nothing. The messenger thinks you would like to know.

effects.log: You sit beside Han Ilseong in the Silent Hall for a year, saying nothing. It is the only kind of visit they would want.

choices.text: Teach their name at the conference

effects.log: You teach ten thousand immortals the name of Han Ilseong. It is remembered again, in many mouths.

events.text: Han Ilseong did not fade. They came back to your conference, a little thinner, and sat in their place. And this time, when the last lecture began, they stayed for it.

choices.text: Give the last lecture to them

effects.log: Han Ilseong stands at the front and says nothing for an hour. Every immortal there remembers it as the clearest lecture of their life.

choices.text: Give the best last lecture of your life

effects.log: You speak for Han Ilseong, who listens. You see them nod once, and that is all you wanted.

events.text: Bang Soyul has left a single cup out on the empty high terrace at the end of the conference, as is their custom, for whoever comes last. This year, it is you. The tea is cold and very good.

effects.log: You drink it on the empty terrace and remember every conference at once.

choices.text: Leave it for whoever is later

effects.log: Somebody later drinks it. You never learn who. Bang Soyul knows, and will not say.

events.text: Saengmo, Mother of Seeds, comes to see how Namu is doing and stays for three lectures. At the end they say, kindly, that your conference reminds them of a forest: a great deal of noise, and everything slowly growing in it.

choices.text: Ask them to lecture on growing

effects.log: Saengmo lectures on patience in seeds. The Still Water and the Open Hand both take notes.

choices.text: Thank them and walk them to the gate

effects.log: You walk the god of Life to the gate. The flowers along the path open as they pass.

events.text: In the place where Han Ilseong always sits, an immortal who did not know has sat down, and the whole terrace is too shy to tell them. Han Ilseong has arrived, and stands a little behind them, perfectly still.

effects.log: The two sit side by side. The young immortal never learns what they almost did. Han Ilseong seems to enjoy the company.
Han Ilseong simply sits on the step below, and from then on that is their place.

events.text: Pungnyeon of the Golden Field, god of the Harvest, sends the conference its tea every cycle now, grown on a hill below the clouds by mortals who do not know who it is for. This year a note has been tucked into the sack, in a child's hand.

effects.log: It says: "I hope it tastes good, whoever you are." Ten thousand immortals drink to the child below.
You send the child below a dream of the terraces and the tea. They grow up to be a tea-grower too.

events.text: Do Yeonhwa, the clerk of the Heavenly Court who brought you the blank page, has asked leave of the Court to attend your conference. The Court refused. They have come anyway, on their day of rest, and sit in the last row with their sleeves still inky.
events.arc: The Clerk of the Book of Fates

effects.log: You greet Do Yeonhwa by name from the high terrace. The Court hears of it, and grants the leave, stiffly.
Do Yeonhwa comes every cycle after that, in the last row, and you never once look. They are very grateful.

events.text: Do Yeonhwa has made a discovery in the Book of Fates. Every immortal who has asked a true question at your conference has a line in the Book that bends a little afterwards, as if fate had to make room. They are frightened by it, and thrilled.
events.arc: The Clerk of the Book of Fates

choices.text: Ask them to keep the count

effects.log: Do Yeonhwa counts the bent lines. There are more of them every century. The Court does not know what to do.

choices.text: Tell them to keep it quiet

effects.log: Do Yeonhwa keeps the secret. Some things grow better unwatched.

events.text: The Court has found out what Do Yeonhwa counted, and has dismissed them from the Book of Fates for meddling. They come to your gate with a bundle of brushes and nowhere to go.
events.arc: The Clerk of the Book of Fates

choices.text: Make them keeper of your conference's records

effects.log: Do Yeonhwa joins Mok Hyeran in the Record of Questions. The two of them argue about ink for a thousand years, happily.

choices.text: Go before the Court for them

ok.log: The Court restores Do Yeonhwa, with a little extra rank, to be rid of you.

fail.log: The Court refuses you. Do Yeonhwa joins your conference instead, and the Court is poorer for it.

events.text: Do Yeonhwa comes at night with the Book of Fates open in their arms. A line in it is bending as they watch: a mortal below, a child, who heard one of your lectures carried down by an immortal and is about to ask a question that will change their whole fate.
events.arc: The Line That Should Not Bend

effects.log: The child asks. The line bends. Do Yeonhwa writes the new fate in, with trembling hands, and it is a good one.

choices.text: Ask what the old line was

effects.log: The old line was short and plain. The new one is long. You decide you do not need to see more.

events.text: Unmyeong the Weaver, god of Fate, has summoned you, politely, to the Silent Hall. They have noticed the bending lines. They are not angry. They want to know how you do it, and whether you would teach the Weaver.
events.arc: The Line That Should Not Bend

effects.log: You teach Unmyeong to ask questions. The Weaver laughs, for the first time in an age, at their own first question.

choices.text: Tell them you do not do it; the askers do

effects.log: Unmyeong is quiet a long time. "Then I will attend," they say. The god of Fate sits in your third row.

events.text: Unmyeong the Weaver has rewoven one thread of the Book of Fates after your lesson: their own. Do Yeonhwa reports it in a whisper. The god of Fate has given themself a question they cannot answer, on purpose, so as to keep learning.
events.arc: The Line That Should Not Bend

choices.text: Send them a cup of conference tea

effects.log: The god of Fate drinks it and writes back one word: "Again."
You take a question you cannot answer and keep it. Your next lectures are better for the not-knowing.

events.text: Your post in the Heavenly Court has brought you a warrant to sign: the Court wants all teaching in heaven licensed, and your conference first. Do Yeonhwa, who drafted it under orders, slips you a note: "Please do not sign it well."

effects.log: The warrant dies on your desk. The Court's ladder is cool to you for a while.

choices.text: Sign it, with your conference exempt

effects.log: The warrant passes. Every small teacher in heaven is licensed except you, and they all come to your conference to complain.

choices.text: Rewrite it so licences are free and certain

effects.log: The warrant passes as a promise: any teacher who asks is licensed. Do Yeonhwa frames the draft.

events.text: Under the warrant, the Court has refused a licence to one teacher: a fallen god who teaches in the ruins of their own domain to anyone who wanders in. The Court says a fallen god may not teach. Do Yeonhwa says that is nonsense.

choices.text: Invite the fallen god to your conference

effects.log: The fallen god teaches on your lowest terrace. Their lecture on loss is the most attended of the cycle.

choices.text: Overrule the Court's clerks with your post

effects.log: You stamp the licence yourself. The fallen god is grateful. The clerks remember.

events.text: Jang Mireu, born a mortal and four centuries immortal, sits in the back row of every conference and takes notes in a script nobody else uses: the plain writing of a mortal schoolroom below. They say the gods' script is too beautiful to think in.
events.arc: The Scholar of the Back Row

effects.log: You learn the mortal script from Jang Mireu. Your next lecture notes are plainer and clearer.

choices.text: Ask them to teach it on a terrace

effects.log: Jang Mireu teaches the plain script to two hundred immortals. Within a century the Court is complaining it cannot read their letters.

events.text: Jang Mireu has written a book of your lectures in the mortal script and sent it down below the clouds. It has been copied a thousand times by mortal schoolteachers, who do not know who wrote it or who first said it.
events.arc: The Scholar of the Back Row

effects.log: Your words are in mortal schoolrooms now, without your name. Faith of a quiet kind rises from below.

choices.text: Ask them to add a line about the source

effects.log: Jang Mireu adds one line: "These were said on a high terrace." It becomes a saying below.

events.text: A mortal schoolteacher below has written a letter to the conference in the plain script, care of Jang Mireu. They have read the book for forty years, and they have a question about the last chapter, and they will die before an answer can come by ordinary means.
events.arc: The Scholar of the Back Row

choices.text: Answer it in a dream tonight

effects.log: The old teacher below dreams your terrace, and your answer. They wake, and write it in the margin, and are content.

choices.text: Send Jang Mireu down with the answer

effects.log: Jang Mireu goes down below and sits with the old teacher to the end. They come back quiet, and gentler.

events.text: Jang Mireu proposes something the conference has never done: a terrace for questions sent up from mortals below, read aloud by an immortal and answered by whoever can. The gods of the Will of Heaven say mortals do not ask about the Dao. Jang Mireu says they ask nothing else.

effects.log: The Terrace of Questions from Below opens. The first question read aloud is why the rain comes late. The god of Thunder answers, embarrassed.
One conference of mortal questions. At the end, the gods vote to keep it. Mujin of the Thousand Banners votes yes, loudly.

events.text: A question has come up from below that nobody on the Terrace of Questions from Below can answer: a mortal child asks why the gods need a conference, if they already know everything. The terrace has gone silent.

effects.log: The answer is carried back below. Mortals everywhere find it strangely comforting.

choices.text: Read it at the opening, beside the stone

effects.log: Cheon Uri's question and the child's are read side by side every cycle after. They are the same question.

events.text: Jang Mireu, now ancient for one born mortal, tells you their immortality is wearing thin, the way the old ones of mortal birth sometimes do. They are not afraid. They would like to sit in the front row, once.

effects.log: Jang Mireu sits in your seat at the opening, in plain robes, and reads Cheon Uri's question in the mortal script.

choices.text: Seat them in the front row, and sit in the back yourself

effects.log: You take their place in the back row and take notes in the plain script. Jang Mireu laughs aloud at the sight.

events.text: Jang Mireu has left the conference for the last time. In the back row they left their notebook, the first one, four thousand years old, written in the plain script of a mortal schoolroom. On the last page is your name and a sentence.

effects.log: It says: "Taught me that a god can be wrong." You keep the notebook by the stone.

choices.text: Put the notebook in the Record of Questions

effects.log: Mok Hyeran's heirs give it its own shelf. Young immortals learn the plain script from it.

events.text: Do Yeonhwa has spilled ink on the Book of Fates, a small blot over a line far in the future. They are white with terror. Under the blot, faintly, the line is rewriting itself around the spill.

effects.log: Do Yeonhwa breathes again. Somewhere ahead, a mortal's fate has a small dark flower in it.

choices.text: Lift the ink with your qi

ok.log: The blot lifts. The line, unhappy at being disturbed, settles back.

fail.log: The blot spreads. Fate makes room for it. Do Yeonhwa forgives you.

events.text: A letter in the plain mortal script has been left on the stone of the first question. It is not from Jang Mireu. It is from one of their pupils, who has learned the script so well that they have forgotten the gods' writing entirely.

effects.log: You answer in the mortal script. It takes you three drafts. The pupil is delighted.

choices.text: Pin it up for the conference

effects.log: The letter is read by ten thousand immortals, slowly, with their lips moving.

events.text: The clerks of the Heavenly Court have asked, very formally, for a holiday on the opening day of your conference. The Court does not grant holidays. Do Yeonhwa says they will all be ill that day, regardless.

effects.log: The Court grants it, sourly. The clerks fill a whole terrace, still in their ink-sleeves.

choices.text: Hold an extra session at night

effects.log: The clerks come after their work, yawning. They are the most attentive terrace you have.

events.text: Mujin of the Thousand Banners, god of War, has come to the conference with a thousand banner-bearers, who stand at attention on every terrace and frighten the young immortals. Mujin wants to learn one thing: how to end a war well.
events.arc: The God of War Takes Notes

effects.log: Mujin sends them home, grumbling. Without them the god of War is shy, and listens.

choices.text: Let the banners stay and learn too

effects.log: A thousand banner-bearers attend a lecture on peace in perfect ranks. Several of them weep.

events.text: Mujin of the Thousand Banners has ended a small war on the edge of heaven by sitting both generals down to the conference tea. They send you a captured banner with no device on it at all, only white silk.
events.arc: The God of War Takes Notes

effects.log: The white banner hangs by the stone of the first question. Mujin visits it more than they visit their own.

choices.text: Send it back with a question

effects.log: You write on the white silk: "And the next one?" Mujin keeps it in their war-tent forever.

events.text: Mujin asks, before the whole conference, whether a god of War should give up war. The young immortals look at you. The banner-gods of the Will of Heaven look at you harder.
events.arc: The God of War Takes Notes

effects.log: Mujin nods slowly. The Will of Heaven relaxes. That century, wars in heaven are shorter.
Mujin goes down below the clouds in disguise for a decade. They come back quieter than anyone has seen them.

events.text: Cheonho, Who Hangs the Stars, god of the Sky, has brought a map of every star they ever hung, and wants the conference to tell them which ones matter. They have hung so many they have forgotten why.

choices.text: Ask them which they hung first

effects.log: Cheonho points, embarrassed, to a very dim star. "For someone," they say, and will not say who.
Each immortal chooses one star. By the end every star has someone, and Cheonho is moved.

events.text: Cheonho tells you who the first star was for: a mortal shepherd, ages ago, who looked up at an empty sky and was lonely. The shepherd is long dust. Cheonho wants to know if the star should be taken down.

effects.log: The dim star stays. Below the clouds, a shepherd looks up at it tonight.
The first star blazes. Cheonho looks younger for a thousand years.

events.text: Hwarin of the First Hearth, god of Fire, offers to light a hearth on your highest terrace, so the conference never goes cold. The Throne of Storms objects. The Green Assembly worries about the trees.

effects.log: The first hearth of heaven burns on your terrace. Immortals gather at it in the evenings, and the best talk moves there.
Hwarin lights a hearth the size of a teacup. It is enough. It is perfect.

events.text: The hearth on your terrace has gone out for the first time in centuries. Hwarin of the First Hearth is distraught. Someone, they say, stopped believing in warmth; a fire of heaven feels that.

ok.log: A young immortal whose teacher died. You sit with them by the cold hearth until it catches again.

fail.log: You do not find them. Hwarin relights it, sadly.

choices.text: Relight it with your own fire

effects.log: The hearth burns again in your colour. Hwarin is grateful and a little jealous.

events.text: Baekun the Pale Ferryman, god of Death, comes to the conference in a grey hood and rows a little boat around the edge of the terraces through the clouds. Every immortal is careful not to look. At the end, they ask you one question: "Do they hate me?"

effects.log: The Ferryman lowers the hood, and rows home slower.
Ten thousand immortals wave to the god of Death. The Ferryman does not know what to do, and waves back.

events.text: Baekun the Pale Ferryman asks to give a lecture, on rowing. Only rowing. The conference is terrified. Your best students hide in the back.

effects.log: The god of Death lectures on rowing: the patience of it, the far shore. Nobody is afraid at the end.
You row the Ferryman's boat around the conference while they rest. You understand something about the oar.

events.text: Mongsa the Sleeper, god of Dreams, has attended your conference asleep. They lie on a cloud at the edge of the lowest terrace and, by the third day, half the young immortals are dreaming the lectures they missed.

effects.log: The conference has a dreaming terrace now. Some of the best questions come from it.
Mongsa wakes, and blinks, and says the conference is better in person. They stay awake for a whole cycle.

events.text: You dream your own conference, as Mongsa has dreamt it. In the dream every immortal is a child, asking, and you are a child too, sitting on the stone, not knowing.

choices.text: Stay in the dream a while

effects.log: You wake with a child's question in your mouth, and ask it at the next lecture. It is the best question of the cycle.
Your lectures afterwards are shorter, plainer, and easier to dream.

events.text: Horang, Lord of the Wild, god of Beasts, has come to the conference in the shape of a vast striped tiger and lain down across the great stair. Nobody can get up or down. Horang appears to be asleep.
events.arc: The Lord of the Wild Sits Down

effects.log: You step over the god of Beasts. One eye opens. Horang is amused, and moves.

choices.text: Sit down beside them and wait

effects.log: You sit by the tiger for a day. At evening Horang says: "You are the first who did not ask me to move." They stay for the whole conference.

events.text: Horang, Lord of the Wild, has sent the conference a student: a fox spirit who has learned to speak and now will not stop asking questions. The fox has already been thrown out of three lectures.
events.arc: The Lord of the Wild Sits Down

choices.text: Give the fox a seat in the front row

effects.log: The fox asks forty questions in one lecture. Thirty-nine are good. The fortieth is about dinner.
The fox becomes the most patient student you have ever had, once someone answers.

events.text: Haeryong, Keeper of Tides, god of the Sea, has come to the conference with a tide. It rises up the lowest terrace in the mornings and down again at night, and immortals have begun to hold lectures knee-deep in it.
events.arc: The Tide Comes to the Terraces

choices.text: Ask them to keep the tide

effects.log: Your conference has a tide now. The young immortals learn that a lecture can be interrupted by the sea, and go on.

choices.text: Ask them to take it home

effects.log: Haeryong takes the tide home, a little hurt. They send a shell in apology for asking.

events.text: The tide of Haeryong has brought something up the terraces: a drowned question, very old, written on a tablet from a conference held by some god long before you, under the sea. Nobody can read it.
events.arc: The Tide Comes to the Terraces

ok.log: It is Cheon Uri's question, word for word, asked an age before Cheon Uri was born.

fail.log: You cannot read it. Haeryong takes it back to the deep, promising to bring it again.

choices.text: Put it by the stone unread

effects.log: The drowned tablet sits by the stone of the first question, wet every morning, unreadable.

events.text: Noegong of the Nine Drums, god of Thunder, cannot keep quiet: every time a lecture moves them, a drum sounds. Half the conference is deafened. The other half claps along.

choices.text: Ask them to save it for the end

effects.log: Noegong saves every drum for the closing. The thunder at the end of the conference is heard to the mortal world below.
You time your lecture to the drums. The immortals learn when they should feel something.

events.text: Noegong of the Nine Drums confesses that they have only eight. The ninth was lost in the War in Heaven of an older age, and its silence is why they drum so much. They have heard your conference has a stone for questions.

choices.text: Let them strike the stone, once

effects.log: Noegong strikes the stone of the first question. It sounds like the ninth drum. The god of Thunder sits down and is quiet for a century.

choices.text: Ask the immortals to make a ninth drum

effects.log: The immortals make a drum of terrace wood. It sounds wrong, and Noegong loves it more than all the others.

events.text: Daeak of the Unmoving Peak, god of the Mountains, has never moved. They have sent word that they would like to attend your conference, and have begun, very slowly, to walk. They will arrive in about two hundred years.

choices.text: Send them a herald every year

effects.log: A herald walks beside the god of the Mountains for two centuries, telling them what was said.
You hold one conference on the slope of the Unmoving Peak. Daeak is so moved that a valley forms.

events.text: Daeak of the Unmoving Peak has arrived. They sit at the foot of your terraces, larger than all of them, and ask in a voice like stones settling: "What have I missed?"

effects.log: Daeak laughs, and the conference shakes, and nobody minds.

choices.text: Tell them everything, from the start

effects.log: You tell the mountain every lecture since they began walking. It takes nine years. Daeak listens to every word.

events.text: Pungnyeon of the Golden Field, god of the Harvest, has sent the conference a loaf of bread baked from the first grain of heaven. It is enough for every immortal, no matter how many come. The Silent Hall is suspicious of it.

effects.log: Ten thousand immortals eat the first bread of heaven. The conference is unusually good-natured.

choices.text: Save half for the mortals below

effects.log: Half the loaf goes down below the clouds. A famine there ends quietly that year.

events.text: Unmyeong the Weaver, god of Fate, sits in your third row and knits. It is not fate; it is a scarf. They say it is very restful not to know how it will turn out.

choices.text: Ask them to knit one for the stone

effects.log: The stone of the first question wears a scarf every winter after that.
"I do not know," says the god of Fate, delighted. "Is that not wonderful?"

events.text: For the first time, every one of the twelve gods of the domains is at your conference in one cycle. The heralds are beside themselves. The gods are polite to each other in the way of very old neighbours who never quite forgave a thing.

effects.log: Twelve gods in a circle, and you outside it. They talk to each other all night.
Every god of heaven sits among students for a week. It does them all a great deal of good.

events.text: {sov_war_a} and {sov_war_b} are at war, and the date of your conference has come. Immortals sworn to both sides are on the golden roads to your terraces, and the Court asks whether you mean to hold it at all.

choices.text: Hold it, and declare the terraces neutral

effects.log: The conference opens under a white banner. Enemies sit three rows apart and listen to the same lecture.
The conference waits. Without it, the war has nothing to stop for, and goes on longer.
You set the stone of the first question down between the two hosts. Neither will attack across it.

events.text: Two immortals, one sworn to {sov_war_a} and one to {sov_war_b}, have been seated side by side by accident at the conference. They have spent the lecture arguing in whispers about the Dao, and by evening they are friends. Their generals have each demanded them back.
