effects.log: They go back together, and tell both hosts what was said. A truce of nine days follows.
They stay on the terraces as your students. Both hosts call it desertion. Both are wrong.

events.text: The war between {sov_war_a} and {sov_war_b} has reached the foot of your terraces. A general asks leave to march across the conference: it is the shortest road. The general has, they say, the utmost respect for learning.

choices.text: Refuse, and stand on the stair

effects.log: You stand on the great stair. The general looks at you for a long time, and takes the long road.

choices.text: Allow it, if they stop for a lecture

effects.log: The whole host stops for an hour's lecture on the Dao of the Road. Half of them do not march on.

choices.text: Turn the road with your Dao

ok.log: The road bends around your conference, and the host never notices.

fail.log: The road resists you. The host marches through, carefully, and breaks only a teacup.

events.text: {sov_student} has been called up by {sov_war_a}. They come to you in armour that does not fit, and ask if a student of yours should fight.

effects.log: {sov_student} goes to the war. Every month a letter comes, shorter each time.
You answer to {sov_war_a} for your student. It costs you a great deal at Court, and you would pay it again.
{sov_student} goes, and holds lectures in the camp at night. Soldiers of both sides creep in to listen.

events.text: {sov_student} has come back from the war between {sov_war_a} and {sov_war_b}. They are not wounded. They sit on the stair and cannot remember why they used to love the conference.

choices.text: Sit with them, and say nothing

effects.log: You sit on the stair for a season. One evening {sov_student} asks for a cup of tea, and you know they will be all right.

choices.text: Give them a lecture to prepare

effects.log: {sov_student} lectures on what they saw. It is the most terrible lecture ever given on your terraces, and the most needed.

events.text: The Thrones of heaven are at war, and {sov_realm} has sent an envoy to your conference: whoever holds the Throne at the end will need the blessing of the Grand Dao Conference. The envoy is offering a great deal to know which side you will bless.

effects.log: The envoy goes away confused. Both sides spend the war wondering what that means.

choices.text: Ask the envoy to stay for a lecture

effects.log: The envoy stays, and listens, and does not go back. {sov_realm} sends another.

choices.text: Promise to bless whoever keeps the peace longest

effects.log: Both sides try to keep a peace to win your blessing. It is not a good reason, but it is a peace.

events.text: The war of the Thrones has ended, and the new holder of {sov_realm} climbs your terraces in full regalia, to ask for the blessing of the conference before all heaven.

choices.text: Seat them in the back row, like anyone

effects.log: The new Throne sits in the back row, and is laughed at, and stays, and is better for it.

choices.text: Give the blessing, with a question in it

effects.log: You bless the Throne with a question it must answer every century. It has not answered it yet.

events.text: Each of the four pantheons wants its own table at the conference: the Will of Heaven a bright one, the Silent Hall a dark one, the Green Assembly one that grows, the Throne of Storms one that thunders. They have been arguing about it for a decade.

effects.log: One table, four pantheons, a great deal of shouting, and by the end some real conversation.

choices.text: Give them four, and sit at none

effects.log: Four tables. You eat on the steps. The pantheons all come to the steps to talk to you.
Gods of the Silent Hall beside gods of the Will of Heaven. The first night is terrible. The second is the best of the age.

events.text: Two gods from rival pantheons, seated together by your plan, have written a joint treatise on the Dao of Light and Shadow. Both pantheons are scandalised. The treatise is very good.

choices.text: Read it aloud at the opening

effects.log: The pantheons are scandalised more loudly, and read it in private, all of them.

choices.text: Give it to the Record of Questions

effects.log: Mok Hyeran's Record has its first treatise. The two gods visit it together every century.

events.text: {sov_pantheon} has made you an offer: take a seat at its council, and the Grand Dao Conference will be its conference, with all the faith and glory of a pantheon behind it.
events.arc: The Pantheon That Wanted the Conference

choices.text: Refuse: the conference belongs to no one

effects.log: The pantheon is offended, briefly. Its gods still come, as students, which is all you ever wanted.

choices.text: Accept a seat, not a claim

effects.log: You sit on {sov_pantheon}'s council, and the conference stays yours. It is delicate for a thousand years.

choices.text: Ask every pantheon to sponsor it equally

effects.log: All four pantheons pay for the tea. None of them can claim it. The tea is excellent.

events.text: {sov_pantheon} has begun sending only its own gods to your lectures, and sitting them in the front rows early, so that other pantheons must sit behind. The Green Assembly has complained in a thunderstorm of leaves.
events.arc: The Pantheon That Wanted the Conference

choices.text: Clear the front rows each morning

effects.log: Every morning the front rows are cleared and filled by lot. {sov_pantheon} complains. Then it laughs.

choices.text: Give the front rows to mortals-born

effects.log: The front rows go to immortals born below. No pantheon can argue. They all try.

events.text: {sov_accused}, whom the Heavenly Court has accused, has come to your conference and sat in the third row. The Court has sent a warrant officer after them, who waits at your gate, unwilling to enter.
events.arc: The Accused in the Third Row

choices.text: Let the officer in, after the lecture

effects.log: The officer waits a day, and then listens to the end of the last lecture before making the arrest. They are gentle about it.
Your terraces are a sanctuary from that day. The Court is furious. Many come who are not guilty of much.

ok.log: "To ask one question before the trial." They ask it. You answer. They go to the officer at peace.

fail.log: They will not say. They leave before the last lecture, and the officer follows.

events.text: The trial of {sov_accused} has begun before the Heavenly Court, and the defence has asked for you as a witness: of character, they say, though you only saw them once, in the third row.
events.arc: The Accused in the Third Row

effects.log: You tell the Court how they listened. It is a small thing. The Court's sentence is a little lighter.

choices.text: Refuse to judge one you taught

effects.log: The Court accepts your silence. The accused writes to thank you for it.

events.text: An exile of the Heavenly Court is at your gate: a god stripped of their seat for a crime that most of heaven has forgotten. They ask, without much hope, to attend the conference.

effects.log: The exile sits on the lowest terrace. By the end of the cycle three gods have spoken to them, which is three more than in a century.

choices.text: Let them in, and ask them to lecture on exile

effects.log: The exiled god lectures on being forgotten. Cheon Uri, of all people, weeps.

events.text: The Court has written to you about the exile on your terraces: it is not forbidden, it says, but it is noticed. The exile offers to leave so that you do not suffer for them.

effects.log: The exile stays. The Court notices, and lets it go. You sleep well.

choices.text: Accept, and find them a quieter place

effects.log: You find the exile a seat at a small conference of your students far away. They thrive there.

events.text: The Throne of Storms has sent its gods to debate the Dao of Weight at your conference, and they argue as their pantheon always does: in weather. It has been raining on the third terrace for a month, and snowing on the fourth.

choices.text: Hold the debate under an awning

effects.log: The debate goes on under canvas, loud and wet. It settles nothing and the immortals love it.

choices.text: Ask them to argue in words, once

effects.log: The storm gods argue in words for an afternoon. They are surprisingly bad at it, and laugh.

events.text: The gods of the Will of Heaven, who cast no shadows, have complained that your terraces are too dim for teaching. The gods of the Silent Hall have complained, the same day, that they are too bright.

effects.log: A bright terrace and a dim one. Most immortals find they think best on the stair between.

choices.text: Tell them both to bring lamps or shades

effects.log: Each pantheon brings its own. The conference looks like a festival.

events.text: An immortal who lost their companion in the War in Heaven has climbed the terraces to ask the conference one thing: whether the Dao has any use for grief. Nobody on the terrace moves.

effects.log: You tell them something you have never told anyone. They nod, and stay for the whole conference.
One by one, immortals stand and say what grief taught them. It takes all night.

events.text: The Heavenly Court has asked you to lecture its officials on the Dao, as part of the ladder of promotion. They come in rank order, with notebooks, and want to know what will be on the examination.

choices.text: Tell them there is no examination

effects.log: The officials are horrified, then curious. Some of them learn something.
You set them Cheon Uri's question. The Court's promotions stop for a century.

events.text: A small sect below the clouds, which you blessed once from the conference terraces, has written up to you. Since the light fell on their mountain, every disciple has broken through, and the elders are afraid it has made them soft.

choices.text: Tell them the light is for beginning, not for ending

effects.log: The elders read your letter aloud in the courtyard, and set the disciples to the hard way again, gladly.

choices.text: Send them a teacher from the conference

effects.log: A patient immortal goes down to the mountain. The sect grows slower and much deeper.
More light. More breakthroughs. The elders do not write again.

events.text: The sect you blessed has grown proud. Its disciples tell other sects below that they are the chosen of a Supreme God, and have begun to settle quarrels by saying so. A smaller sect nearby has written to you too, to complain.

choices.text: Answer the smaller sect, and bless it too

effects.log: Two sects in the light now. The proud one is furious, then ashamed, then friendly.

choices.text: Send a dream to the proud disciples

effects.log: Every disciple of the proud sect dreams the same night of sitting in your back row, unnoticed. They wake humbler.

choices.text: Let them learn on their own

effects.log: The proud sect loses its next three quarrels. It learns.

events.text: The founder of the sect you blessed has ascended at last and climbed the clouds all the way to your conference. They kneel at the gate and will not rise until you tell them whether the sect was worthy of the light.

choices.text: Raise them, and seat them as a student

effects.log: "It was," you say, "because it asked." The founder takes a seat in the third row and never leaves.
The founder thinks for a long time. "Mostly," they say. You laugh, and so do they.

events.text: Do Yeonhwa of the Book of Fates, or a clerk like them, has noticed the mark you wrote in the margin of a life not yet begun: your own next birth, made a little better with what the conference taught you. They ask, carefully, what it means.

choices.text: "That I will start again, and learn more."

effects.log: The clerk writes it down beside the mark. The Book accepts it.
The clerk smiles. Somewhere ahead, a teacher you do not know yet is waiting.

events.text: In a dream you see a little of the life you have marked: a child somewhere, on a hill, asking an adult why the sky is so far away. The adult does not know. The child keeps asking.

effects.log: You wake smiling. Whatever comes, it will be asked about.

choices.text: Write the question in the Record

effects.log: Mok Hyeran's Record has one question in it that has not been asked yet.

events.text: The disciple you raised with your enlightenment has stood up from their breakthrough, shaking, and asked you the question every raised disciple asks: whether the realm is truly theirs, or only lent.

effects.log: The disciple stands straighter. They never ask again.
They spend a century earning it. When they have, they thank you for the word lent.

events.text: The disciple you raised has gone further than you raised them, on their own. They come to the conference and sit in the back row so as not to be seen with their teacher. Everyone knows anyway.

effects.log: You call them by name. The disciple comes forward red-faced, and the terraces applaud.
They stay in the back, contented. Later they say it was the first time they felt they belonged.

events.text: The disciple you raised has raised a disciple of their own, with enlightenment they earned themselves. The new one is brought to you as a courtesy. They have no idea who you are.

choices.text: Introduce yourself as nobody in particular

effects.log: The new disciple chats with you for an hour about their teacher, who is wonderful. You agree.

choices.text: Give them a cup of the conference tea

effects.log: They drink it and pull a face. Your disciple laughs: they pulled the same face once.

events.text: A temple of yours below the clouds has stopped burning incense. Instead its priests have begun to hold small gatherings every few years where anyone may bring a question and argue it out. They write, worried, to ask if this is allowed.
events.arc: The Temple That Became a School

choices.text: Tell them it is the best worship

effects.log: The temple becomes a school. Its faith in you does not fall. It changes colour.

choices.text: Ask them to burn one stick too

effects.log: One stick of incense at each gathering. The priests are relieved; the arguers do not notice.

events.text: The temple-school below has copied your conference so well that mortals now climb its steps from three kingdoms away. One of them asks the priests Cheon Uri's question without ever having heard of Cheon Uri.
events.arc: The Temple That Became a School

choices.text: Send the answer you would give Cheon Uri

effects.log: The priests receive your answer, which is "I do not know." They are disappointed, then delighted.
The priests answer it badly, and the mortal goes home thinking hard. That is the point.

events.text: Among the prayers rising to you from below is one that asks for nothing. It is a question, the same one, every night, from the same mortal: "What did you learn today?"
events.arc: The Prayer That Was a Question

effects.log: You answer every night, in a sentence. The mortal writes your sentences down. After forty years it is a book.
You send the question back in a dream. The mortal laughs in their sleep and answers.

events.text: The mortal who asked you every night what you learned has grown old below. Their last prayer is not a question. It is a list of everything they learned from your answers.
events.arc: The Prayer That Was a Question

effects.log: It takes an hour. You did not know you had taught so much in a sentence a night.

choices.text: Grant them a good next birth

effects.log: You mark the old mortal's next life in the margin of fate: a teacher, somewhere.

events.text: A mortal sculptor below has made a statue of you for a temple, and given it, for reasons of their own, a teacup in one hand and an open palm in the other. The priests are not sure it is dignified.
events.arc: The Statue with an Open Hand

choices.text: Bless the statue as it is

effects.log: The statue with the teacup becomes the most loved in the kingdom below. Children leave tea in the cup.

choices.text: Send the sculptor a dream of the terraces

effects.log: The sculptor dreams your conference, and makes a second statue: ten thousand small figures listening.

events.text: Children below leave tea in the cup of your statue, and the priests have noticed that whoever drinks it afterwards asks better questions for a day. They want to sell it.
events.arc: The Statue with an Open Hand

effects.log: The tea stays free. The priests grumble and then forget to mind.

choices.text: Let them sell it for the poor

effects.log: The tea is sold for coppers, and the coppers feed the poor of the town below.

events.text: A priest of yours below has invented a new incense that burns in the shape of a question mark. Mortals queue for it. The Heavenly Court has asked, drily, whether this is your doing.

effects.log: The Court rolls its eyes. The incense spreads to nine kingdoms below.

choices.text: Say it was the priest's idea

effects.log: The priest is famous for a while below, and very pleased.

events.text: The light of your blessing has fallen, by some trick of the clouds, on the wrong mountain: a band of mortal robbers below, who woke with the sudden urge to sit down and think about their lives.

effects.log: Half the robbers become a small, odd sect. The other half become farmers. Nobody is robbed.

choices.text: Move it to the right mountain

effects.log: The light moves. The robbers go back to robbing, puzzled.

events.text: Hundreds of mortal children below dream the same dream on the same night: a high terrace, a stone with words on it, and a god pouring tea who looks up and smiles at them. Their parents bring offerings to every temple they can find.

choices.text: Hold a lecture for the dreamers

effects.log: For one night your conference has a terrace of sleeping mortal children. You teach them to ask.

choices.text: Ask Mongsa the Sleeper what happened

effects.log: The god of Dreams admits it left a door open. They close it, gently, for next time.

events.text: The people of {sov_world}, your Pocket World, have heard of the Grand Dao Conference from the heroes you sent down to them. They have built a copy of your terraces out of wood, very small, and hold their own conference every few years.

effects.log: You sit in the back of the little conference of {sov_world}. A farmer gives the best lecture you have heard in a century.

choices.text: Send them a stone for their first question

effects.log: A stone from your own terrace falls gently into {sov_world}. They carve a question on it you have never thought of.
The little conference grows on its own. Faith rises from {sov_world} like warm air.

events.text: The little conference of {sov_world} has sent you its question, carved on the stone you gave it: "Does the god who made us have a god who made them?" It has gone up to the Grand Dao Conference, where nobody can answer it either.

choices.text: Read it beside Cheon Uri's question

effects.log: Two questions stand on the stone now. Nobody can tell which is older.
You answer: "I do not know, and I am asking." {sov_world} is comforted to have a god who asks.

events.text: A student from the little conference of {sov_world} has ascended out of the Pocket World entirely, the first ever, and climbed to your real terraces. They are astonished to find them so large, and the tea so strong.

choices.text: Seat them in the front row

effects.log: The student of {sov_world} sits among gods and is not afraid. They ask the best question of the cycle.
They go back down to {sov_world} and tell everyone what the real terraces are like. Nobody believes them about the tea.

events.text: An old figure in a plain robe has sat at the back of your conference for three days and asked nothing. On the fourth day the heralds realise, and fall on their faces: it is the Dao Ancestor, descended, attending as anyone would.
events.arc: The Ancestor at the Back of the Hall

effects.log: You finish the lecture you were giving. The Dao Ancestor nods once, and you will never know what for.
The Dao Ancestor laughs, a sound like the first spring. "Ask me again when I know," they say.
The Dao Ancestor declines your seat. "I came to sit at the back," they say. "It has been too long since I did."

events.text: The Dao Ancestor has left a gift on the stone of the first question: nothing at all. A bare place on the stone, smooth as water, where something used to be carved and is not. The conference argues about it for a century.
events.arc: The Ancestor at the Back of the Hall

effects.log: The smooth place is the most visited spot in heaven. Nobody touches it.

ok.log: You read it in the stone's memory: an older question, the Ancestor's own. You keep it.

fail.log: The stone keeps its secret. You find that you are glad.

events.text: The masters of the Clone Forge have offered to forge a body for you, so that you could lecture on two terraces at once. Your students are excited. Mok Hyeran thinks it is a very bad idea.

effects.log: Two of you lecture on two terraces. Both lectures are good. Neither is quite you.
"A teacher is in one place," you say. Mok Hyeran writes that in the Record, with a satisfied flourish.

events.text: The forged body lectured on the second terrace and, by the end, answered a question you would have answered differently. A student asks you, very seriously, which of you was right.

effects.log: The student is shaken, then fascinated. They study both answers for a century.
The body returns to the Forge. You keep its answer, in a small box, unread.

events.text: The keepers of the Heavenly Calendar have written to say that your next conference falls on the same day as the festival of Hwarin of the First Hearth, the oldest feast in heaven. One of you must move.
events.arc: The Date on the Heavenly Calendar

effects.log: You move. Hwarin is so pleased that they bring the feast to the next conference instead.
A conference with a feast in it. Lectures are shorter and louder. Everyone remembers it.

events.text: The keepers of the Heavenly Calendar have asked, shyly, whether they could mark your conference as a feast day of its own: the Day of the First Question. It would be the first day in the Calendar that belongs to no god.
events.arc: The Date on the Heavenly Calendar

choices.text: Agree, if it belongs to no one

effects.log: The Day of the First Question is marked in the Calendar under no god's name. Immortals everywhere ask a question that day.

choices.text: Ask for it to be Cheon Uri's day

effects.log: The Calendar marks the Day of Cheon Uri. They are mortified and very moved.

events.text: The keepers of the Tower ask you to set a trial on one of its divine floors: not a beast or a guardian, but a question, that every climber must answer to go higher.
events.arc: A Lecture on the Divine Floor

effects.log: Climbers stand on your floor for years. The few who say "I do not know" are let through.

choices.text: Set a question that changes for each climber

effects.log: Your floor asks each climber what they least want to be asked. The Tower has never been so slow.

events.text: A climber of the Tower has been standing on your floor for four hundred years. They have not given up, and they have not answered. The keepers ask whether you will let them pass out of pity.
events.arc: A Lecture on the Divine Floor

effects.log: You sit beside the climber. After a year they laugh, and say "Oh," and walk up the stair.
In the five hundredth year, the climber answers. The answer is new, and you write it in the Record.

events.text: One of the four Elder Lineages of heaven, whose blood is older than the Court, has sent its youngest heir to your conference, with a retinue of forty and a list of things the heir must not be taught.
events.arc: The Elder Lineage Sends a Child

effects.log: The heir arrives alone at the next session and asks forty questions from the forbidden list.

choices.text: Read the list aloud at the opening

effects.log: The whole conference hears what an Elder Lineage fears. The heir is mortified and grateful.
You teach around every forbidden thing. The heir learns most from the shape of what is missing.

events.text: The heir of the Elder Lineage has gone home and been questioned by their elders, and has told them, firmly, that your conference is the only place in heaven that does not care whose blood they have.
events.arc: The Elder Lineage Sends a Child

effects.log: The elders of the Lineage come, stiffly, and sit in the back. One of them asks a question. The Lineage is never quite the same.

choices.text: Let the heir carry the conference home

effects.log: The heir starts a small conference of their own inside the Lineage, in secret, for cousins.

events.text: A letter comes from the Court of the Unlit Sun, the court of heaven that meets in darkness and answers to none of the pantheons. It asks for one seat at your conference, in the shadow, for an envoy who will not show their face.
events.arc: A Letter from the Unlit Sun

effects.log: The envoy of the Unlit Sun sits in the shadow of the stone for the whole conference, and takes notes in the dark.

choices.text: Grant it, if the envoy asks one question aloud

effects.log: The envoy asks: "Is a question asked in the dark still a question?" You answer yes, and they bow.
The envoy does not come. The next cycle, the shadow by the stone is a little deeper anyway.

events.text: The envoy of the Court of the Unlit Sun has left a gift in the shadow by the stone: a lamp that gives no light, only makes it easier to think. Your students are fighting over who may sit by it.
events.arc: A Letter from the Unlit Sun

choices.text: Give it to the Still Water

effects.log: Seo Dohwan's school sits by the dark lamp in silence. They say it is like the still pool.

choices.text: Give it to the Terrace of Argument

effects.log: Your loudest terrace becomes, by the dark lamp, quiet enough to hear itself.

events.text: The Concord of Domains, where the gods of the twelve domains settle their borders, has asked to meet on your terraces between conferences. They say it is the only place in heaven where gods remember to listen.
events.arc: The Concord Meets on the Terraces

effects.log: The Concord meets on your stone steps. Two border quarrels are settled before tea.

choices.text: Lend them the terraces, and the tea-master

effects.log: Bang Soyul, or whoever keeps the kettle, brews for the Concord. Three quarrels are settled.

events.text: The Concord of Domains has asked you to break a deadlock: two gods claim the same river. Each has a long list of reasons. They have agreed, astonishingly, to accept your judgement.
events.arc: The Concord Meets on the Terraces

choices.text: Ask them each a question instead

effects.log: You ask each god what the river is for. Their answers are the same. They share it.

choices.text: Give the river to the mortals below who drink from it

effects.log: The river belongs to no god. Both gods are outraged, then relieved.

events.text: A child of {sov_world} has written a letter to the god who made their world and sent it up on a kite. It asks if you have a teacher, and if so, whether your teacher is kind.

effects.log: You write about Cheon Uri, and your students, and the stone. The child of {sov_world} keeps the letter for a lifetime.

choices.text: Send a kite of your own down

effects.log: Your kite comes down in {sov_world} with a cup of tea tied to it. The child drinks it and makes a face.

events.text: A climber who passed your floor of the Tower has come down again, all the way, just to tell you that the question on your floor was harder than everything above it.

effects.log: They tell you. You set a new question on your floor the next day, a little kinder.
They drink it on the stair and begin climbing again in the morning.

events.text: Two of the four Elder Lineages have quarrelled about who should sit nearer the stone of the first question. Each claims its blood was there before the stone was carved.

choices.text: Tell them the stone was carved last week

effects.log: You recarve one letter, freshly. Neither Lineage can claim to be older than it.

choices.text: Seat them both in the back

effects.log: Both Lineages sulk in the back row, together. They end up friends.

events.text: A teacup broke at your lecture and you went on talking with the pieces in your hand. Now a whole school of young immortals calls itself the Broken Cup and teaches that every lesson begins with something lost.
events.arc: The School of the Broken Cup

effects.log: The Broken Cup holds its first lectures among shards. They are thoughtful and rather gloomy.

choices.text: Tell them you were just distracted

effects.log: The Broken Cup takes this as the deepest teaching of all. You give up.

events.text: The School of the Broken Cup has begun breaking cups on purpose, to begin lessons properly. Bang Soyul, or whoever keeps the kettle now, has run out of cups and is threatening to resign.
events.arc: The School of the Broken Cup

choices.text: Tell the school to mend one cup a day

effects.log: The Broken Cup becomes the School of the Mended Cup. Its lectures grow warmer.

choices.text: Give them clay and a kiln

effects.log: They must make every cup they break. They break far fewer, and learn a great deal about clay.

events.text: The School of the Broken Cup, or Mended Cup, or whatever it calls itself this century, has sent its founder to ask you what the first cup was. They have been arguing about it for three hundred years.
events.arc: The School of the Broken Cup

choices.text: Tell them the truth: an ordinary cup

effects.log: The founder is crushed, then delighted. The school makes a pilgrimage to the kitchen.

choices.text: Give them the pieces, which you kept

effects.log: You kept them. The founder holds them in both hands and cannot speak.

events.text: Your youngest herald, sent down the golden roads with the invitations for the next conference, has lost them in a cloud. They come back in tears. The conference is in a month and nobody knows it is happening.
events.arc: The Herald Who Lost the Invitations

choices.text: Hold it anyway, for whoever comes

effects.log: Forty immortals come, by chance. It is the closest conference you have ever held.
The invitations go out late and in a rush. The conference is full and chaotic.
You find the cloud. It has read every invitation and would like to attend. You let it.

events.text: The herald who lost the invitations has become the most careful herald in heaven, and now asks to be trusted with the invitations to the Dao Ancestor and the four pantheons. The older heralds are appalled.
events.arc: The Herald Who Lost the Invitations

effects.log: Every invitation arrives. The pantheons remark on the beautiful handwriting.

choices.text: Send them with an older herald

effects.log: The two go together and argue the whole way. Every invitation arrives twice.

events.text: An immortal has stood up at your conference and given a brilliant answer to a hard question. Too brilliant: Mok Hyeran recognises it, word for word, from a lecture of the rival conference a century ago, which the immortal did not attend.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Bought an Answer

choices.text: Ask them, gently, where they learned it

effects.log: They confess they bought the notes from a clerk. They are ashamed. You ask them to explain the answer. They cannot.

choices.text: Praise the answer, and the one who first gave it

effects.log: You name the true source aloud. The immortal goes grey and sits down.
The immortal is applauded. They do not sleep for a decade.

events.text: The immortal who bought an answer has come back, years later, with an answer of their own to the same question. It is clumsy and wrong in one place. It is theirs.
events.arc: The Immortal Who Bought an Answer

choices.text: Praise it more than the first

effects.log: You praise the clumsy answer before the whole conference. The immortal weeps openly.

choices.text: Show them where it is wrong

effects.log: They mend the wrong place. The answer is now better than the bought one.

events.text: The great stair up to your conference has worn hollow in the middle from ages of feet. The masons of heaven want to replace it with a new one of jade. The old immortals are against it; they say the hollow is the history.

effects.log: The stair stays hollow. New immortals stumble on it and learn to look down.

choices.text: Build the new one beside it

effects.log: Two stairs. The young take the jade. The old take the hollow. They meet at the top.
A jade stair, perfect and cold. You miss the hollow at once.

events.text: Someone has been carving tiny questions into the treads of the great stair, one per step, so that climbers read them on the way up. There are nine hundred steps. They have done four hundred.

effects.log: In a century the stair is a book of nine hundred questions. Immortals climb it slowly now.

ok.log: It is Cheon Uri, of course. They are embarrassed. You hand them a better chisel.

fail.log: You never catch them. The questions keep appearing.

events.text: The date of the conference came and nobody climbed the stair. Not one immortal. A great storm on the golden roads, the heralds say, or a festival elsewhere, or simply chance. You sit on the stone with the tea going cold.

choices.text: Give the lecture anyway, to the terraces

effects.log: You lecture to empty terraces for a day. It is the most honest lecture you have ever given.

choices.text: Go down the stair yourself and find them

effects.log: You walk the golden roads and lecture to whoever you meet. It is the widest conference ever held.

events.text: A century after the cycle nobody came, an immortal tells you they were on the stair that day, at the very bottom, and turned back because they thought they were not ready. They have regretted it ever since.

choices.text: Tell them what you said that day

effects.log: You give them the lecture you gave the empty terraces, word for word. They write it all down.
They sit down on the step, as if a weight had come off them.

events.text: A god only forty years old, born of a new mountain spring below the clouds, has climbed to the conference and sat in the front row. The ancient gods behind them are offended. The child god has brought a slate and chalk.
events.arc: The God Who Was Too Young

effects.log: The child god asks the questions nobody else dares to. The ancient gods take notes, grudgingly.

choices.text: Ask the ancient gods to tutor them

effects.log: Each ancient god teaches the child one thing. By the end of the cycle the child god knows more than most.

events.text: The child god of the mountain spring has stopped coming. Their spring dried up below, in a drought, and the god is fading with it. They send a chalk note: "Thank you for the front row."
events.arc: The God Who Was Too Young

choices.text: Go below and bring the rain

effects.log: You ask Noegong of the Nine Drums for one storm. The spring runs again. The child god comes to the next conference, soaked and laughing.

choices.text: Teach them to hold on without the spring

effects.log: You teach them to be a god of a memory of water. They hold on, thinner, and come back.

events.text: A single embroidered slipper has been left on the high terrace after the conference, very old, the kind worn by gods of the Silent Hall a thousand years ago. Nobody claims it.

effects.log: It is still there at the next conference. And the next. It has become part of the terrace.

choices.text: Send it to the Silent Hall

effects.log: A thank-you note returns, unsigned, written very small. The handwriting is a thousand years old.

events.text: A young immortal heckles your lecture exactly as Gwak Taeseong once did: "The Dao is not taught. It is taken." The old immortals in the front rows turn round, delighted, to see who it is.

choices.text: Invite them to give the next lecture

effects.log: They give it. It is terrible and brave. You suspect they will be back.

choices.text: Tell them who said it first

effects.log: The young immortal is crestfallen to learn it is not new. They come back with something that is.

events.text: It rains on the conference for the first time in an age, hard, and nobody runs for cover. Ten thousand immortals sit soaked on the terraces, because you have not stopped speaking, and they do not want to miss a word.

effects.log: They shelter, laughing. The lecture goes on under the eaves, wet and cheerful.
You abandon your notes and lecture on rain. It becomes one of the famous lectures.

events.text: On one terrace, someone has discovered, every question echoes back a moment later in a slightly different voice, as if the stone itself were asking it again.

effects.log: Your lecture comes back to you a breath later, a little wiser. You learn from yourself.
The young immortals ask the echo everything. Some of the answers are very strange.

events.text: The first snow of a thousand years falls on the stone of the first question during the opening, and settles in the carved letters, so that for one morning the question is written in white.

choices.text: Let it melt on its own

effects.log: You watch the white question until noon, when it melts. Nobody speaks.

choices.text: Read it aloud, as written in snow

effects.log: Everyone remembers the year the question was read in snow.

events.text: Two immortals who have attended every conference since the first sit on the steps comparing how you have changed. They do not know you are standing behind them. One says you used to be clever. The other says you are wiser now.

effects.log: They are mortified, and then all three of you laugh. You ask which they preferred.
You walk away, pleased with the second one, and a little sorry for the first.

events.text: Halfway through a lecture you realise you have been teaching something wrong for six hundred years. Ten thousand immortals are writing it down.

effects.log: You stop, and say it. The terraces are silent, then they applaud for a long time.

choices.text: Finish, and correct it next cycle

effects.log: You correct it at the next conference. Fewer people hear, and fewer are hurt.

events.text: A student has left a jar by the stone for questions too shy to ask aloud. It is full by the third day. Most are about loneliness, and one is about whether you ever get tired.

effects.log: You answer it at the opening: yes, often. A sigh of relief goes across the terraces.
You write a reply to each and leave them in the jar. It takes a month.

events.text: An immortal who cannot speak attends your lectures and writes questions on a slate. Today the slate says only: "Why do you talk so much?"

effects.log: You teach for an hour without a word. The slate says: "Better."
You tell them you are afraid of silence. They write: "Me too, once."

events.text: A fire in a dormitory of the conference has burned a thousand years of a student's notes. They sit in the ash, unable to remember a single lecture.

effects.log: You give the student your lecture notes, all of them. They are messier than anyone expected.

choices.text: Ask what they remember without notes

effects.log: They remember one sentence. It is the one that mattered. They start again from it.

events.text: A crane spirit has stood on one leg at the edge of the lowest terrace for every lecture this cycle. On the last day it puts its other foot down and bows.

effects.log: You bow to the crane. It flies off, and comes back each cycle with another crane.
The crane answers in a single cry that makes the whole terrace go quiet.

events.text: The conference has run out of ink. Ten thousand immortals with brushes and no ink stare at you, and you have not even begun the lecture.

effects.log: Nobody writes a word. Afterwards, everybody remembers the lecture better than any other.

choices.text: Send to the Court for ink

effects.log: The Court sends ink and a bill. The lecture starts late and is written down perfectly.

events.text: In the front row, a student is fast asleep through your most important lecture of the century. Their neighbours are trying to wake them without you noticing.

effects.log: You lecture quietly so as not to wake them. The whole terrace leans in to hear. It is the best-heard lecture of the age.
They wake and answer it, half-dreaming, rather well.

events.text: You have lost a debate at your own conference, to a young immortal who was simply right. The terraces wait to see whether you will take it well.

effects.log: You concede at once. The young immortal is more shaken than you are.

choices.text: Ask them to take your next lecture

effects.log: They give your lecture, terrified. They are right again.

events.text: A mortal-born immortal asks if you would give one lecture in the plain tongue of the world below, so that those who came up from it can hear the Dao in the words they were born with.

effects.log: Your plain-tongue lecture is clumsy. The mortal-born immortals weep at it all the same.

choices.text: Ask them to translate as you go

effects.log: Two voices on the terrace, yours and theirs. Theirs is the better one.

events.text: You spill a whole pot of tea over the stone of the first question at the opening. The carved letters fill with tea and shine. Some immortals decide it is a sign.

effects.log: The Day of Spilled Tea becomes a custom. You regret this a little.
Everyone laughs. It is a much warmer opening than usual.

events.text: You were going to lecture on the Dao of Emptiness and, standing up, you find you have nothing to say about it at all.

choices.text: Stand in silence for the hour

effects.log: Nobody leaves. Afterward the Still Water says it was the best lecture on emptiness in history.
The questions are better than your lecture would have been.

events.text: You have forgotten the name of a student you taught for three hundred years. They are standing in front of you, smiling, waiting to be greeted.

effects.log: They laugh, and tell you, and forgive you, and you never forget it again.

ok.log: It comes back to you just in time. You say it warmly.

fail.log: It does not come. They see it in your eyes, and are kind.

events.text: A student presents you with a scroll copied by hand: every question you have ever asked them, in order, over four hundred years. The first ones are very foolish.

effects.log: You read your own foolish questions to the conference. Everyone feels braver.
You read it at night, alone, and laugh, and once or twice wince.

events.text: Two schools of your conference are quarrelling about what you meant in a lecture you gave five hundred years ago. You no longer remember what you meant.

effects.log: Both schools are scandalised, then delighted: now the meaning is theirs.
You choose. The other school grumbles, and writes a better reading still.

events.text: On the last night, every immortal lights a lantern with one thing they learned written on it, and sends it up into the sky over heaven. Cheonho, Who Hangs the Stars, complains that they are confusing the stars.

choices.text: Ask Cheonho to keep a few

effects.log: Cheonho hangs nine lanterns among the stars. They are still there.
The lanterns drift down below the clouds. Mortals find them and wonder.

events.text: A very old immortal in the back row has asked the same question at every conference for a thousand years: "Why?" Just that. You have answered it a different way every time.

choices.text: Answer it the same way as the first time

effects.log: The old immortal smiles for the first time in a thousand years. "Ah," they say. "Again."
They think about it all through the conference, and leave with a light step.

events.text: Forged invitations to your conference have been sold below the clouds to mortals, who have climbed for years to reach the gate, clutching them. The forger has vanished. A hundred mortals stand at the gate.

effects.log: A hundred mortals sit on the lowest terrace. One of them asks a question that silences the gods.

choices.text: Send them home with a blessing

effects.log: They go back down with good health and a story. The forger is found below, ashamed.

events.text: You lecture under a tree that grew from a seed dropped at the first conference. Its bark is carved with the initials of immortals who have since ascended or faded.

effects.log: You carve your initial low, by the root. Students find it later and are moved.
You read them all. Some, nobody else remembers. Now they are remembered.

events.text: The great bell that opens every conference has cracked. The bell-founders of the Throne of Storms say it will take a century to cast another.

effects.log: Cheon Uri opens the conference by calling out the question. It carries further than the bell ever did.
The cracked bell rings flat and strange. Everyone agrees it sounds honest.

events.text: An immortal arrives at the last hour of the last day, having walked for nine years, and finds the conference over. They sit down on the stair and do not cry.

effects.log: You give one lecture to one immortal on the empty terraces. They walk home lighter.

choices.text: Give them a seat at the next one

effects.log: You give them a seat by the stone at the next conference. They are the first to arrive.

events.text: A student sobs through your lecture, in the third row, trying to be quiet. Their neighbours pretend not to notice. You are lecturing on joy.

effects.log: You stop. You sit with them on the step. The lecture on joy is never finished, and nobody minds.

choices.text: Go on, and find them afterward

effects.log: Afterward you find them. They say the lecture helped. You are not sure how.

events.text: A student you taught three thousand years ago comes back, now the founder of a pantheon's school of their own. They sit in the back row out of old habit, and get up when you look at them, out of older habit.

choices.text: Ask them to sit down again

effects.log: They sit, smiling. For an hour they are a student again, and rest.
They lecture brilliantly. You recognise one of your gestures, and three of their own.

events.text: A whole terrace misheard your last lecture and has spent a century studying "the Dao of Rivers" when you said "the Dao of Rivals". Their treatise is very good.

effects.log: They are mortified. Then they write a treatise on rivals, too, and it is also good.
You lecture on rivers for them. It turns out you had things to say.

events.text: A student asks you to sum up all your teaching in three words, for a mortal child below who asked them. The terraces lean in.

effects.log: The three words go down below the clouds and are carved over a schoolroom door.
The child below laughs, and drinks, and later understands.
The child is delighted. So is Cheon Uri, when they hear.

events.text: You have lost your voice on the morning of the opening. Not to illness: you simply cannot find it. It happens to gods who have talked for too many thousand years.

choices.text: Let a student read your notes

effects.log: A student reads your notes aloud, nervously. The conference listens to them with great kindness.

choices.text: Write your lecture in the air

effects.log: You write the lecture in light above the terraces. It is remembered as the Silent Year.

events.text: The stone of the first question is warm today, as if someone has been sitting on it all night. Nobody admits to it. There is a faint smell of incense from the Silent Hall.

effects.log: The stone stays warm under you all day. You feel, oddly, accompanied.

choices.text: Leave a cup of tea beside it

effects.log: The next morning the cup is empty and rinsed.

events.text: The Still Water and the Open Hand have fallen out over the tea again: one wants it plain, the other wants it with flowers. Bang Soyul's heirs have refused to choose.

effects.log: You drink a cup of each before the conference. Both schools claim you prefer theirs.
Peace, of a kind. Both schools complain on alternate days.

events.text: You count the students on the terraces this cycle and find that none of them was born when you hosted your first conference. Not one.

choices.text: Tell them about the first night

effects.log: You tell them about Cheon Uri and the cold tea. They listen as if to an old song.

choices.text: Say nothing, and learn their names

effects.log: You learn as many names as you can. It takes the whole conference.

events.text: A paper crane has landed on your lectern with a question folded inside it, unsigned, in a child's hand: "Do gods have teachers?"

effects.log: You tell the conference about every teacher you ever had. Some of them are in the room.

choices.text: Fold an answer and let it fly

effects.log: Your crane flies off over heaven with your answer. You never learn where it lands.

events.text: A student of yours has broken through to a realm above some of the gods in your audience. The gods are uneasy. The student is more uneasy still, and keeps sitting in the back.

effects.log: The student sits among gods, terrified. The gods, after a while, ask them questions.

choices.text: Tell the gods to come and sit in the back

effects.log: Twelve gods squeeze into the back row. Nobody can see, and everybody laughs.

events.text: A scripture has appeared among the immortals called The Sayings of the Supreme of the Terraces. You did not write it. About half of it is things you said. The other half is things you would never say.

effects.log: You denounce the false half. The true half becomes more loved for it.
You trace it to a lonely immortal who wanted their own thoughts to be heard, and put your name on them.
You write in the margins: "Said", "Not said", "Wish I had said." The annotated edition is everywhere.

events.text: The lonely immortal who wrote the false half of your sayings stands before you. Their thoughts, under their own name, were never read. Under yours, ten thousand immortals have argued about them.

choices.text: Let them lecture under their own name

effects.log: They lecture. The terraces are thin at first. By the end, full.

choices.text: Tell them the good parts were good

effects.log: You name the good parts. They weep. They stop writing in your name.

events.text: The Heavenly Court has forbidden you, politely, to lecture on one subject: whether the Court itself is part of the Dao, or only a thing gods built. Every immortal at your conference now wants to hear exactly that.

choices.text: Obey, and lecture on everything around it

effects.log: You lecture on everything except the Court. Everyone understands exactly what you meant.
You lecture on the Court. It is fair and gentle and the Court never forgives it.

choices.text: Ask the Court to send someone to lecture on it

effects.log: A Court official lectures on the Court. It is long, and dull, and more revealing than they meant.

events.text: Copies of your lecture on the Court have been circulating in the halls of the Court itself. A senior official comes to you privately, not to complain, but to ask what you would change.

effects.log: They listen, and write. A century later, one small rule of the Court is gentler.
They have a list. It is longer than yours.

events.text: A student of yours went down below the clouds three centuries ago, to teach in the mortal world, and has not written in a hundred years. Their friends on the terraces are worried.

effects.log: You go down below in a plain robe and follow their trail through mortal towns.

choices.text: Send a herald with a letter

effects.log: The herald finds them and comes back with an answer: "I am well. I am busy. Come and see."

events.text: You find your lost student below the clouds, grey-haired in a mortal body by choice, teaching children in a small school beside a river. They see you at the door and are not surprised.

effects.log: "This is home," they say, kindly. You stay a week, and help with the lessons.
You sit at the back of a mortal schoolroom and learn something about patience you had not learned in heaven.

events.text: One of the children your lost student taught below has ascended. They climb to your conference and present a letter from their old teacher: "This one asks better questions than I did. Be patient."

effects.log: The child of the river school asks the stone's question in their own words, and the terraces go quiet.

choices.text: Write back to the teacher below

effects.log: You write: "You were right." The letter goes down, and is framed in a river school.

events.text: A young immortal begs you to raise them a realm with your enlightenment, as you have raised others. They are talented, impatient and very sure they are ready.

effects.log: You raise them. They stand in a realm too large for them, dizzy and delighted.
"It will be yours," you say, "if you walk it." They storm off, and walk it, slowly.
You open the door a little. They have to push it the rest of the way themselves.

events.text: The immortal you raised too fast has made a mistake that only someone of their new realm could make: they bent a small river of the Green Assembly the wrong way with one careless thought, and the forest is drying.

choices.text: Mend it with them, not for them

effects.log: You and the young immortal bend the river back together. It takes a year. They are quieter after.
The Mother of Seeds is kind and terrible. The young immortal comes back changed.

events.text: The immortal you once refused to raise has walked the realm on their own, slowly, over two centuries. They come back to show you, and to say they were furious with you for a hundred years.

effects.log: "Now I understand," they say. "And I am still a little furious." You both laugh.

choices.text: Give them the tea you would have given then

effects.log: You give them the tea. They drink it, and say it tastes better now.

events.text: A popular teacher on your third terrace has been telling their students that every one of them will reach the highest realm. It is not true. The students are very happy and very diligent.

effects.log: The teacher stops. Half the students leave in grief. The ones who stay work harder still.
"Because they would not try otherwise," they say. You are not sure they are wrong.
The students climb further than anyone expected, on a lie. You are uneasy for a century.

events.text: One of the students of the kindly lying teacher has reached the top of their road, far short of the highest realm, and knows it. They come to you, not angry, only puzzled about what to do now.

choices.text: Tell them the truth, and what it is worth

effects.log: "You walked further than you would have," you say. They think about it, and choose to keep walking.
Teacher and student sit together a long time. The teacher teaches differently after.

events.text: Every immortal who has ever attended your conference dreamt of it on the same night: the terraces, the stone, the tea. In the dream there was one more terrace than in the waking world, and nobody could climb to it.

effects.log: The god of Dreams says the terrace is where the conference is going. It is not there yet.
You build a new terrace to match the dream. Nobody climbs it. It feels, oddly, like a promise.

events.text: The dream of the missing terrace came again, and this time someone climbed it: a figure with no face, sitting on a stone with no words. Many dreamers woke afraid. Some woke laughing.

choices.text: Climb it yourself in the dream

ok.log: You climb, and sit beside the faceless figure, and understand that it is every student you will ever have.

fail.log: You wake at the foot of the stair. The terrace is still waiting.

choices.text: Tell the dreamers not to be afraid

effects.log: You tell the conference it is only the future. Most of them are comforted.

events.text: An immortal arrives with a heavy chest of faith and lays it at your feet: payment, they say, for every lecture they attended in four hundred years. They cannot bear to owe a god.

effects.log: "Nothing was owed," you say. They take the chest away, troubled, and come back to every conference after.

choices.text: Accept it for the mortals below

effects.log: The faith is spent on a famine below. The immortal is astonished, and satisfied.

choices.text: Accept it, and pay them back in tea

effects.log: You give them a cup of tea for every lecture. It takes a decade. They are cured of owing.

events.text: The immortal who could not bear owing has started a custom among their students: nobody pays, but everybody teaches one other person for every lecture they hear.

effects.log: From then on, every immortal who attends teaches one other. The conference doubles in a century.
Their students become the most generous school in heaven.

events.text: An oracle of the Silent Hall has prophesied that your conference will end one day, the stone broken and the terraces empty. Your students are horrified. The oracle looks at you to see what you will do.

effects.log: You thank them. "Then every conference until then is a gift," you say. The students calm.
The oracle smiles. "Another one," they say, "somewhere else." You are content.

events.text: You dream of your own first teacher, long ago, before you were a god. In the dream they are sitting in your back row, taking notes, and they look up and nod.

effects.log: You give your next lecture as if they were in the back row. It is your best in a century.
You sit beside them in the back row and listen to yourself lecture. It is a strange and gentle night.

events.text: The Green Assembly has voted, after nine hundred years of deliberation, to send a delegate to your conference. The delegate is a moss. It will arrive in about three centuries.

effects.log: A damp, shaded corner waits on the lowest terrace. Gardeners of heaven tend it with care.

choices.text: Send a lecture to meet it

effects.log: A herald reads your lectures to the moss as it travels. It arrives very well informed.

events.text: The Throne of Storms has sent a formal apology: one of its younger gods lost their temper at the last conference, and the hail cracked the stone of the first question. The crack runs through the word "who".

effects.log: The cracked "who" becomes the most discussed word in heaven.

choices.text: Ask the young god to mend it

effects.log: The young storm god mends it, slowly and carefully, and learns more than from any lecture.

events.text: The Silent Hall has invited you to lecture in its halls, where no voice is ever raised. They have asked that you lecture in a whisper.

effects.log: Your whispered lecture fills the Silent Hall. The gods of Death and Dreams lean very close.
You teach without a sound. The Silent Hall approves deeply.

events.text: A god of the Will of Heaven confesses at your conference that they have never seen their own shadow, because their halls cast none. They would like to know what it looks like.

choices.text: Stand them by the hearth at night

effects.log: By Hwarin's hearth, the god of light sees their shadow for the first time, and stares at it all night.
You draw the shadow on the stone in charcoal. They keep the drawing forever.

events.text: Auditors of the Heavenly Court have come to count the tea the conference drinks, on suspicion that faith is being wasted. They have counted for a week. They want a cup.

effects.log: The auditors drink, and write "no waste found", and stay for the closing lecture.

choices.text: Make them sit the lecture first

effects.log: The auditors sit through a lecture, scowling, and then ask for two cups.

events.text: A clerk of the Book of Fates has read your own line, against every rule, and come to you shaking. They will not say what it says. They only ask if you would like to know.

effects.log: "I would rather ask," you say. The clerk goes away relieved.

ok.log: The word is "teacher." You smile.

fail.log: The word is one you do not recognise. You spend a century thinking about it.

events.text: The Court has sealed a god for crimes against their worshippers, and the sealed god has sent you, through the seal, a single question: whether a god can learn while sealed.

effects.log: The sealed god spends their sentence learning. When they are released, they come to your back row.

choices.text: Send them a lecture each cycle

effects.log: Your lectures go through the seal, one each cycle. The guards listen too.

events.text: A warrant has come from the Court ordering the conference to use only tea grown in heaven. The tea from the hill below the clouds is very good, and grown by mortals.

effects.log: You keep the mortal tea. The Court sends a second warrant, and then forgets.
You argue for mortal tea for a day. The Court yields, and orders some.

events.text: Hwarin of the First Hearth has asked to marry two of their priests at your conference, by the hearth on your terrace, because the conference is where the two first met.

effects.log: Two priests of Fire are married by the stone. The hearth burns gold.
Ten thousand immortals sing an old mortal wedding song. Hwarin cries sparks.

events.text: Haeryong, Keeper of Tides, has sent seawater for the tea, out of kindness. Bang Soyul's heirs are trying very hard to be polite about it.

choices.text: Drink a cup in front of Haeryong

effects.log: It is terrible. You drink it all. Haeryong is so happy they send a whale to the next conference.
Haeryong laughs at themself, and sends fresh water from a spring under the sea.

events.text: Horang, Lord of the Wild, wants to hold a lecture for beasts at your conference: cranes, foxes, a very old tortoise. The immortals ask if they must sit with them.

effects.log: A fox sits beside a sword immortal. Both learn something about stillness.

choices.text: Give the beasts their own terrace

effects.log: The beasts' terrace is the quietest and most attentive. The immortals are a little embarrassed.

events.text: Daeak of the Unmoving Peak has answered a question asked at your conference two hundred years ago. The answer has only just arrived. The one who asked it has long since ascended.

effects.log: It is a wonderful answer. Somewhere far above, the asker hears it, perhaps.

choices.text: Send it up to the asker

effects.log: A herald climbs out of heaven with the mountain's answer. It is the slowest letter ever sent.

events.text: Noegong of the Nine Drums has decided, after your lecture on silence, to go a whole conference without drumming. The strain is visible. A small cloud follows them around, rumbling.

choices.text: Thank them on the last day

effects.log: You thank them, and the storm breaks: nine drums at once. Everyone cheers.

choices.text: Tell them one drum is allowed

effects.log: One drum, at the best moment. It is perfectly placed.

events.text: Mortal pilgrims below have built a stair of stone up the side of a mountain, as close as they can get to heaven, to leave their questions at the top for you. It ends in cloud.

effects.log: A herald goes down every cycle to bring up the pilgrims' questions. They are often the best.
You answer one question in a thunder that is also a word. The pilgrims are terrified and happy.

events.text: A priest of yours below has written that they no longer believe in you, but would like to keep teaching in your temple, if that is allowed. They have been honest about it with the town.

effects.log: The doubting priest teaches for forty years. Faith in the town rises, oddly.

choices.text: Send them a question to doubt with

effects.log: You send the priest Cheon Uri's question. They write back: "Now I believe in the question."

events.text: Mortals below have begun to keep a festival on the Day of the First Question: children ask their parents anything at all, and the parents must answer truthfully or say "I do not know."

effects.log: The festival spreads to nine kingdoms below. Faith in you rises in a strange shape.
A child below asks you why the sky is blue. You say you do not know. The parents are impressed.

events.text: An old soldier-immortal of a long-ago War in Heaven has asked to teach the youngest students how to lose. Not to fight: to lose, well.

effects.log: The Terrace of Losing is the most crowded of the century.
You learn to lose, from a veteran. You have needed it for a long time.

events.text: Two generals who fought on opposite sides of an old War in Heaven meet by accident at the tea-urn on your terrace. They stand looking at each other with their cups.

effects.log: You fill both cups. They drink together, without a word. Then with many.
They talk all night. In the morning they leave together.

events.text: An heir of an Elder Lineage asks, before the whole conference, whether their blood makes them closer to the Dao. Their elders, in the front row, wait for your answer.

effects.log: The elders are offended. The heir looks lighter than they have in years.
The heir meditates on it for a decade. They come back with an answer the elders cannot argue with.

events.text: The Court of the Unlit Sun has asked whether your conference could, once, be held entirely in the dark, for envoys who cannot bear the light.

effects.log: A lecture in total darkness. Many immortals say they have never heard so clearly.

choices.text: Hold it at the new moon

effects.log: The new-moon lecture becomes a custom. The envoys come every cycle.

events.text: At the Concord of Domains two gods have been arguing for a month over whose domain the conference tea grows in. You have been asked to settle it.

choices.text: Grow a new bush on the border

effects.log: One bush on the line between domains. Both gods water it. Both claim it.

choices.text: Say the tea belongs to whoever drinks it

effects.log: Both gods are appalled. Both drink it.

events.text: A star has fallen onto the high terrace in the night, still warm, with a question written in light on its surface that fades as you watch.

ok.log: It asks whether you remember the first night. You do.

fail.log: It fades before you can read it.

effects.log: Cheonho hangs it back in the sky, a little lower than before.

events.text: A newly ascended immortal arrives at the conference and, seeing you, falls on their face and cannot get up. They have worshipped you since they were a mortal child.

choices.text: Sit down on the ground with them

effects.log: You sit beside them on the stone. After a while they sit up, and laugh, and you talk.

choices.text: Give them a job pouring tea

effects.log: They pour tea for a whole conference, too busy to be afraid. By the end they ask a question.

events.text: A minor god whose domain is the edge of puddles has come to ask your blessing, as if you were a pantheon. They have brought an offering of one perfectly round pebble.

choices.text: Accept the pebble and bless them

effects.log: You bless the god of puddle-edges. They are radiant. The pebble sits on the stone.

choices.text: Ask them to teach you about puddles

effects.log: They lecture for an hour on puddles. It is surprisingly profound.

events.text: The Heavenly Court has offered you a great seat on its ladder, near the top, if you will close the conference for a thousand years to take it up.

effects.log: You refuse. The Court is baffled. The conference opens on its date, as always.

choices.text: Ask if the conference can come to the Court

effects.log: The Court declines, horrified. You keep the conference and no seat.

events.text: The four pantheons have each sent a gift to the conference in the same cycle: a lamp from the Will of Heaven, a silence from the Silent Hall, a seed from the Green Assembly and a wind from the Throne of Storms.

choices.text: Use all four in one lecture

effects.log: Lamp, silence, seed, wind. The lecture is strange and whole.
Each school gets a gift. Each claims theirs was best.

events.text: A temple of yours below has burned in a mortal war. The priests are safe. They have begun to teach in the ruins, under the open sky, and say they rather prefer it.

effects.log: The temple goes up again. The priests leave the roof off one room.

choices.text: Tell them the sky is a good roof

effects.log: The roofless temple becomes famous below. Pilgrims bring their questions to it in the rain.

events.text: A fallen god, whose domain was taken from them in some old war, sits on your lowest terrace every cycle and gives a little lecture to anyone who stays after: on what is left when everything is taken.

effects.log: You sit with the fallen god's handful of listeners. It is the clearest lecture of the cycle.
The fallen god declines kindly. "The lowest is where it belongs," they say.

events.text: The heralds have counted, and this is the hundredth Grand Dao Conference you have hosted. They want to make it magnificent: every god, every pantheon, a feast of a year. You have been asked what you want.

effects.log: It is an ordinary conference, on purpose. Everyone agrees it was the most moving of all.
A year of feasting and lectures. Heaven talks of nothing else for a millennium.
Every immortal who ever came, living or ascended, is asked. Some of the ascended come down.

events.text: At the hundredth conference someone has brought the first teacup, the one you held on the first night, which Cheon Uri kept. It is chipped. They ask you to drink from it at the closing.

effects.log: You drink. The tea is from the first night's leaves, somehow. The terraces are silent.

choices.text: Give it to the youngest present

effects.log: A child god drinks from the first cup, makes a face, and is famous for it ever after.

events.text: Word comes that the immortal who first taught you, before you were a god, before heaven, still lives: a hermit on a forgotten crag of the Upper Realm, who never ascended further.

effects.log: You climb down out of heaven to a forgotten crag. Your old teacher is making soup.
An invitation goes down. It comes back: "Too busy. Soup."

events.text: Your old teacher eats soup with you on the crag and asks what you teach now. You tell them about the stone, and the question, and the ten thousand. They listen, and then ask why you are so tired.

effects.log: You tell them about every student who left, and every one who stayed. They pour more soup.

choices.text: Ask them how they kept from tiring

effects.log: "I only ever had you," they say. "One was enough." You go home thinking.

events.text: Your old teacher has finally come to your conference, at a great age, carried up the stair in a chair by your students. They sit in the back row, and you find you cannot begin.

effects.log: You open the conference with the first thing they ever taught you. It is very simple. It is still true.
Your old teacher stands up in the back and says, "Well? Go on." The whole conference laughs, and you begin.

events.text: The children of {sov_student} have come to the conference for the first time, grown, immortal, and determined not to be impressed by their parent's teacher.

choices.text: Do not try to impress them

effects.log: You are ordinary with them. By the end they are impressed despite themselves.

choices.text: Tell them embarrassing stories of their parent

effects.log: {sov_student} is mortified. The children are enchanted.

events.text: One of the children of {sov_student} has asked a question their parent never thought to ask. {sov_student} sits very still in the third row, astonished and proud and a little stung.

effects.log: You answer, and look at your old student. They nod. They are a teacher too; they understand.
{sov_student} answers their own child before ten thousand. It is not a perfect answer. It is very loving.

events.text: You notice one morning that you have given the same lecture three conferences in a row, and nobody has complained, because nobody remembers the one before. You are very tired.
events.arc: The Weariness of a Long Teacher

effects.log: For the first time ever, the conference does not open. Heaven is anxious. You sleep.

choices.text: Give the lectures to your students

effects.log: Your students teach the whole conference. You sit in the back row, and rest.
You go and sit in the lectures of a school you never attended. You come back with a new lecture.

events.text: Cheon Uri, or whoever keeps the stone, has noticed your weariness. They bring you a list of every question asked at the last conference that you have never answered before. It is a long list.
events.arc: The Weariness of a Long Teacher

effects.log: You read the whole list. Not one is old. You feel young.

choices.text: Choose one and answer it slowly

effects.log: You take a year over one new question. The answer is the best thing you have made in centuries.

events.text: A student of yours has chosen to give up immortality and live out a mortal span below the clouds with someone they love who is mortal. They come to say goodbye, and are not sad.
events.arc: A Student Who Chose a Mortal Span

effects.log: They go down with your blessing. For a century they write, and the letters are happy.
They listen, kindly, and go anyway. You are ashamed of trying.

events.text: The student who chose to live mortal has grown old below, and their letters have stopped. Their grandchildren write instead: their grandparent spoke of a high terrace and a stone, and they want to know if it was real.
events.arc: A Student Who Chose a Mortal Span

effects.log: You write the grandchildren a long letter. One of them grows up to climb the clouds.
You stand at a small grave below with a cup of tea, and pour it on the earth, and stay a while.

events.text: The stone of the first question has worn thin from ages of hands touching it. The carved words are fading. The masons say they can recut them, or carve them on a new stone.

effects.log: The old words are cut deeper. The stone is thinner. It will last a while yet.
The words fade over centuries. Immortals read them by touch. Then by memory.
The question goes onto every stair of the conference. There is no single stone anymore.

events.text: A student has asked, timidly, what will happen to the conference when the stone of the first question is gone altogether. Many others are waiting for your answer.

effects.log: The students nod. That night three of them carve the question into their own doorways.
The students are silent. It is the first time many of them understand it.

events.text: A minor god of the Green Assembly named Yun Ari has come to every conference you ever held, and sat beside you at the closing tea. You realise you have never asked them anything about themself.
events.arc: The God Who Came to Every Conference

effects.log: Yun Ari is the god of the last leaf to fall each autumn. They are delighted to be asked, and talk all night.
"Because you always look as if you need someone at the closing," they say. You are speechless.

events.text: Yun Ari, god of the last leaf, has not come to the closing tea. You find them in a forest of the Green Assembly, very small, holding on to a branch. It is not yet their season to fall.
events.arc: The God Who Came to Every Conference

effects.log: You sit through a winter in a forest. In spring Yun Ari lets go, laughing, and is caught by the wind back to your terraces.

choices.text: Bring the closing tea to them

effects.log: You hold the closing of the conference in the forest, for one guest. They are very touched.

events.text: You try one night to count every student you have ever taught, and cannot. You get to nine hundred thousand names and then begin to forget the first ones.

effects.log: You stop. They are not numbers. You sleep well.
The Record has every name. It is a whole building. You walk through it for a day.

events.text: You dream of a conference held by someone else, where you are only a guest in the back row, and nobody looks at you, and the tea is made badly, and you are utterly happy.

choices.text: Tell your heir about the dream

effects.log: They laugh. Then they promise to make the tea badly for you, one day.
You keep it, like a coin in a pocket, for a hard day.

events.text: It is Cheon Uri's birthday, by the reckoning of a god nobody remembers. Nobody else on the terraces knows. They are sitting alone on the stair with an ordinary cup.

choices.text: Sit with them and say happy birthday

effects.log: Cheon Uri laughs in surprise. You are the first to say it in an age.
Ten thousand immortals sing to Cheon Uri. They hide their face in their sleeves.

events.text: Cheon Uri asks you, privately, whether they ruined your conference by asking a question nobody can answer. They have been afraid of it for centuries.

effects.log: They look at you for a long time. Then they nod, and go back to the stair, lighter.
They ask another. It is also unanswerable. You both laugh.

events.text: Cheon Uri has carved a little statue of the faded god who made them and set it on the lowest terrace. Immortals have begun to leave tea in front of it.

effects.log: You leave a cup. Cheon Uri sees, and turns away to hide their face.

choices.text: Ask the conference what god it is

effects.log: Cheon Uri tells the story. A god is remembered by ten thousand.

events.text: Yeon Seorin has found a new gate of the Dao, in the middle of the great stair, where thousands walk every day. Nobody else can see it. They stand in the way of everyone, patiently.

effects.log: A bench by the invisible gate. Yeon Seorin sits on it. Traffic flows again.
They describe it for an hour. You almost see it.

events.text: Yeon Seorin is sweeping the stair at dawn when you come down. They hand you a second broom without a word.

effects.log: You sweep the whole stair together. It takes until noon. You feel very clear.
"Because the gate is always somewhere," they say, "and it might be here."

events.text: Gwak Taeseong shows a group of young sword immortals an old scar on their palm, from the first sword they ever held. The young ones are disappointed: they expected something from a great duel.

choices.text: Tell them it is the greatest scar

effects.log: You tell them the iron sword is the reason for every other. Gwak looks pleased and gruff.

choices.text: Show them your own oldest scar

effects.log: Yours is from a cooking pot. The young immortals laugh, and then understand.

events.text: Ha Jiwoo has made a net for catching falling stars before they land on the terraces. It is very large and full of holes, and it works.

effects.log: You hang the star-net over the conference. It catches three falling stars in a century.

choices.text: Ask what they do with the catch

effects.log: They hang them back, one by one, under Cheonho's eye.

events.text: Seo Dohwan of the Still Water hands you a smooth pebble without a word, and walks off. The pebble is perfectly ordinary.

effects.log: You carry it for a century. Some days it is very heavy.
You drop it in still water. The ripples do not stop for a long time.

events.text: Ryu Gaeun of the Open Hand meets you on the stair and gives you, with great ceremony, nothing at all. Both their hands are open and empty.

effects.log: You take the nothing with both hands. Ryu Gaeun beams.
You hold out empty hands. Ryu Gaeun laughs so loud the stair rings.

events.text: Mok Hyeran, keeper of the Record of Questions, has a question for you to add to the Record. They have never asked you anything before. They ask: "Are you happy?"

effects.log: You answer. Mok Hyeran writes down the question and not the answer, as is the rule.
They think about it a long time. "Yes," they say, surprised. They write that down, against the rule.

events.text: Bang Soyul tells you, at last, the secret of the conference tea: there is none. The leaves are ordinary. They only wait a little longer than seems right.

effects.log: You never tell. The tea stays legendary.

choices.text: Teach it at the next lecture

effects.log: You lecture on waiting longer than seems right. It is the most practical lecture you ever gave.
