events.text: One of Namu's leaves has fallen on your lectern, with a word on it you cannot read. The Green Assembly says it is a word you will need later.

choices.text: Keep it pressed in a book

effects.log: The pressed leaf waits in your book of lectures. One day you will read it.
Saengmo reads it and smiles and will not tell you. "Later," says the Mother of Seeds.

events.text: The pressed flower Han Ilseong gave you from the Silent Hall, where nothing grows, has put out a living root in the drawer where you kept it.

effects.log: A flower of the Silent Hall grows on your terrace, grey and very lovely.

choices.text: Take it back to Han Ilseong

effects.log: You bring it to the Silent Hall. Han Ilseong looks at it for a whole day.

events.text: Do Yeonhwa has been offered promotion in the Heavenly Court, on the condition that they stop attending your conference. They ask what you think, carefully not showing what they want.

effects.log: They take it. A century later they return, senior and still inky, to the last row.
Do Yeonhwa looks at their inky hands and refuses the promotion.

events.text: Jang Mireu has found a spelling mistake in the carved question on the stone of the first question. It has been there since the first night. Nobody else has ever noticed.

effects.log: The mistake stays. Jang Mireu adds a tiny note in the plain script beside it, which is also misspelt.
You correct it. The stone looks wrong for a century, and then looks right.

events.text: Seo Dohwan and Ryu Gaeun, both very old now, sit together on the high terrace in the evening, saying nothing and holding cups. Their schools have stopped quarrelling, mostly.

effects.log: Three old teachers in a row, in silence. Every student who passes is careful not to disturb them.
You leave them. From below, you see one of them laugh.

events.text: Cheon Uri and {sov_heir} have met for the first time, on the stair. The one who asked the question and the one who will carry your Dao look at each other with great curiosity.

effects.log: You introduce them. They talk all night about you, which is unnerving.
They walk off together, already arguing.

events.text: Yeon Seorin, who waited nine thousand years at a gate, and Gwak Taeseong, who never waited for anything, have been seated side by side. Both are trying very hard to be polite.

effects.log: By the end of the conference Gwak is waiting for things and Seorin is interrupting. Both are improved.
The lecture on patience and impatience is a disaster and a triumph.

events.text: A spark from Hwarin's hearth has caught a shelf of the Record of Questions. Mok Hyeran, or their heir, is fighting it with a teapot.

choices.text: Put it out with your qi

ok.log: The fire dies at a word. Not one question is lost.

fail.log: The fire dies, but one shelf is ash. Mok Hyeran's heir begins rewriting from memory.

choices.text: Carry the shelves out by hand

effects.log: You carry the questions out of the fire, armful by armful. Your robe is singed.

events.text: Bang Soyul, long retired, comes back to the terraces for one day and makes one pot of tea. Only one. They pour it for you, and then for the stone.

effects.log: You drink the last pot of Bang Soyul's tea together. Neither says anything.

choices.text: Ask them to come back every year

effects.log: They come back every year for one pot. It is always for you and the stone.

events.text: You find Gwak Taeseong, very old, standing alone under the crooked star that bears their name, pretending not to be moved.

effects.log: You stand under the star together. Gwak says "Stupid star," and does not leave for an hour.
You leave quietly. Later Ha Jiwoo tells you Gwak stayed all night.

events.text: Do Yeonhwa and Mok Hyeran, who keep the Record of Questions together, are not speaking. One wants questions filed by date. The other by who asked them. The Record has two indexes and they disagree.

choices.text: Ask them to file by what was meant

effects.log: A third index. Both are appalled. They reconcile in order to oppose it.
They sort it out in a century. The Record has two indexes, forever.

events.text: Han Ilseong of the Silent Hall, who has spoken once in your hearing, is seen whispering to Namu by the stone. The tree rustles. Neither will tell you what was said.

effects.log: You do not ask. That evening Namu drops a leaf at your feet.
Namu rustles. Han Ilseong looks almost amused.

events.text: Jang Mireu has brought rice cakes from a mortal market below to the conference, wrapped in leaves, the way their mother made them, long ago. There are exactly enough for the front row.

choices.text: Give yours to the back row

effects.log: You pass yours back. Everyone passes theirs back. The last row eats them all and cries.
It is very good. Jang Mireu watches you eat it with great satisfaction.

events.text: Cheon Uri has begun a new small book. On the first page, instead of an answer, they have written a list of every person who said "I do not know" to them, with the date. Your name is first.

effects.log: It is long now. Most are children. Some are gods.
You tell them of a mortal teacher below who said it to you once. Cheon Uri adds the name.

events.text: {sov_student_b} has come back from long wandering with a staff, a beard of dust and very little to say. They sit in their old seat as if they had never left.

choices.text: Pour them tea without a word

effects.log: They drink it. "Still too hot," they say. You smile.
"Questions," they say. "So many." You both look at the stone.

events.text: {sov_heir} has made the conference tea for the first time, and made it badly, on purpose, because you once said in a dream you would like that.

effects.log: It is terrible. You drink it all. {sov_heir} watches you, pleased with themself.

choices.text: Show them how, one more time

effects.log: You make it together, the long way. {sov_heir} pretends to need the lesson.

events.text: A letter from {sov_strival} arrives, written centuries ago and lost on the golden roads. It says: "I was wrong about one thing. Not the rest." It does not say which thing.

effects.log: You write. The answer comes a century later: "You know which." You do.
The conference argues for a decade about which thing. {sov_strival} is delighted.

events.text: You understand something enormous about the Dao of Time while washing a teacup. The cup is still wet in your hand. There is nobody to tell.

effects.log: You finish the cup. The insight stays. You teach it next cycle, starting with the cup.
You run, dripping, and try to explain. Half of it is lost on the way. The half that arrives is very good.

events.text: A century-long meditation of yours is interrupted on its last day by a student knocking to ask if you want lunch.

effects.log: You have lunch. The last day of meditation was, it turns out, the lunch.

choices.text: Ask them to wait one day

effects.log: They wait. When you come out, they have made lunch for a hundred.

events.text: You realise that your Dao has quietly changed shape over the millennia. It is no longer the Dao you walked to become a god. It has become the Dao of Teaching.

effects.log: You accept the change. Your next breakthrough comes in a lecture, mid-sentence.

choices.text: Look back for the old Dao

ok.log: You find it, under the new one, like a road under snow. Both are yours.

fail.log: You cannot find the old road. You walk on.

events.text: Your enlightenment has grown so full that it spills: the tea brewed near you tastes of clarity, and students sitting close to your seat break through without meaning to.

effects.log: You sit further from the front. Breakthroughs become their own again.
A whole terrace breaks through in one season. The Court asks questions.

events.text: For a decade, nothing you teach lands. The students nod politely. You feel the enlightenment in you lying quiet as a pool in a windless valley.

effects.log: You listen for a decade. Then one student's question breaks the stillness.
You teach on into the quiet. One day it lands again, and you are glad you kept going.

events.text: You are asked to lecture on the Dao of the Sword, which is not yours. The sword immortals in the front row are waiting with crossed arms.

choices.text: Admit it is not yours, and ask them

effects.log: The sword immortals lecture you instead. It is the best sword lecture of the age.

choices.text: Lecture on it as a stranger would

ok.log: Your outsider's view surprises them. They uncross their arms.

fail.log: They are polite, and unconvinced.

events.text: Students of the Dao of Flame ask you how to keep a fire burning for ten thousand years. Hwarin of the First Hearth is in the front row, which does not help.

effects.log: Hwarin answers in one word: "Feed it." The students are disappointed and then thoughtful.
A practical lecture. The fire students light small fires for a century afterwards.

events.text: A student of the Dao of the Void has asked you what is in the void. The terraces are very still. It is a test.

effects.log: The student laughs. The terraces breathe again.

choices.text: Sit in silence until they answer it

effects.log: They answer it after a year. You agree.

events.text: A student of the Dao of Time asks whether you would go back and teach the first conference differently, if you could.

effects.log: The student is surprised. You explain about cold tea and honest mistakes.

choices.text: "Everything. Which is why I teach now."

effects.log: They write it down. It becomes a saying of the Dao of Time.

events.text: A student of the Dao of Karma asks you, with great seriousness, how much karma you have made by teaching. They have tried to calculate it and failed.

effects.log: They are scandalised. You suggest they stop counting too. They try.

choices.text: Ask them to count it for you

effects.log: They work on it for a century and give up, smiling.

events.text: A student of the Dao of Water asks how to teach someone who does not want to learn. Haeryong, Keeper of Tides, is listening from the tide-pool on the lowest terrace.

choices.text: "As water does. Slowly, and by staying."

effects.log: Haeryong makes the tide come in, approvingly.
The Keeper of Tides says, "Wait for them to be thirsty." It is the shortest lecture of the conference.

events.text: A student of the Dao of Earth has come with a stone from their home world below and asked you to teach them what it knows. Daeak of the Unmoving Peak watches from the foot of the terraces.

effects.log: You hold it an hour. The student holds it an hour. You both learn the same nothing, together.
The mountain holds the little stone and tells it something. The student never forgets the sound.

events.text: A student of the Dao of Illusion has replaced the conference with an illusion of itself as a test, and you have been lecturing to it for an hour before you notice.

effects.log: You finish, to the illusion. The student, watching from outside, is mortified and impressed.
You praise it. The student is so pleased they let you out at once.

events.text: A student of the Dao of Life asks you why anything should die, if the Dao is whole. They have just lost their teacher. They want an answer, not a lecture.

effects.log: You sit with the student until they sleep. It is the only answer you have.
The Mother of Seeds takes them to a forest where everything is dying and growing at once.

events.text: A student of the Dao of Thunder can only learn while shouting. The terraces around them have emptied. They are very sorry, very loudly.

choices.text: Teach them on the storm terrace

effects.log: You lecture them in a storm, both of you shouting. It is the happiest lecture of the cycle.
It takes a century. They whisper like distant thunder now, and the terraces fill again.

events.text: A student of the Dao of Balance has stood on one foot on the edge of the high terrace for forty days to prove a point. Nobody remembers what the point was.

effects.log: They come down and fall over. Both of you laugh. The point is made.

choices.text: Stand on one foot beside them

effects.log: You stand forty more days with them. You both forget the point.

events.text: A student of the Dao of Space asks how big your conference really is. They have measured it and the numbers keep coming out different.

effects.log: They measure again with that in mind. The numbers agree, for once.
You measure it together all night and get a new number each time. It is a lovely night.

events.text: A student of the Dao of Slaughter has come to the conference in a plain robe, asking if their Dao has any place on your terraces. Everyone has moved away from them.

choices.text: Seat them in the front row

effects.log: They sit in the front row, terrified of themselves. Their questions are the most careful in heaven.

choices.text: Ask them what they want to learn

effects.log: "How to stop," they say. You spend a century on that, together.

events.text: You break through mid-lecture. The light is visible on every terrace. Ten thousand immortals stop writing to stare.

effects.log: You finish the sentence you were in. Then you sit down. It is the most quoted lecture of the age.
You laugh, uncontrollably, in light. Some of the students begin laughing too, and do not know why.

events.text: A storm of qi has gathered over your terraces after a great lecture, from ten thousand insights at once. The clouds are thick with understanding and very low.

effects.log: Understanding rains on the terraces. The students soak it up, literally.

ok.log: You draw the storm in. Your understanding swells, wide as a sky.

fail.log: The storm is too much. It breaks over you and leaves you dizzy for a year.

events.text: You talk in your sleep, your students tell you, and what you say is questions. They have been writing them down for a century. They want to know if they may teach them.

effects.log: The Sleeping Questions become a book. You cannot answer most of them.
You read your sleeping self's questions. Some are better than your waking ones.

events.text: An immortal artisan has made a mirror that shows not your face but the shape of your Dao. In it you are a terrace, a cup and a question, all at once.

effects.log: Every student looks in it on the way in. Many are surprised by their own shape.

choices.text: Look in it once, and give it back

effects.log: You look once. You give it back. You did not need to see it twice.

events.text: On the seventh day of a fast, a word comes to you that you have never heard and that is clearly yours. You do not know what it means.

effects.log: You keep the word. Sometimes, lecturing, you feel it in your mouth.
You teach a word you do not understand. The students understand it for you.

events.text: You have been sitting on a cloud above your terraces for a year, watching the conference without being seen. You have learned more about your teaching than from a thousand lectures.

effects.log: You change half your lectures. The students are puzzled and much better taught.
You come down satisfied. It was good. You only needed to see it.

events.text: You offered a share of your enlightenment to an immortal who was failing, and they refused it. They want to fail on their own, they say, and then perhaps succeed.

effects.log: You withdraw the gift. They fail, and fail, and then succeed, and come to thank you for not helping.
You leave the gift where they can reach it. They never take it. That is also an answer.

events.text: You have half an insight: the first half. It has been sitting unfinished in your mind for three hundred years. A student has just said the second half by accident.

effects.log: You tell them they finished your thought. They are astonished, and you share the insight, half and half.

choices.text: Keep it, and thank them oddly

effects.log: You thank them with great feeling for a remark about the weather. They are puzzled for a century.

events.text: You have asked the Dao itself a question, directly, in deep meditation, for the first time in your life. You are not sure if the silence after is an answer.

effects.log: You take the silence as an answer. It sits well with you for a thousand years.

ok.log: The second silence is different. You understand the difference. You never ask a third time.

fail.log: The silence is the same. You laugh at yourself.

events.text: The four pantheons have each asked to host one cycle of your conference in their own realms: in the bright halls of the Will of Heaven, the grey pools of the Silent Hall, the forests of the Green Assembly and the crags of the Throne of Storms.

effects.log: The conference packs its stone and its kettle and sets off across heaven.
The pantheons come to you instead, sulkily, and bring their realms in their sleeves.

events.text: The conference in the bright halls of the Will of Heaven has gone strangely. With no shadows, nobody can tell when someone is hiding a doubt. Lectures are confident and shallow.

choices.text: Bring a lamp of shadow from the Unlit Sun

effects.log: One lamp, and the hall has shadows. The questions get harder at once.

choices.text: Teach on the beauty of certainty, then doubt it

effects.log: A lecture in two halves. The gods of the Will of Heaven are shaken and grateful.

events.text: In the forests of the Green Assembly the conference took eleven years, because nobody could hurry the trees, and the trees had questions. Your immortals are restless. The trees are only getting started.

choices.text: Stay until the trees are done

effects.log: You stay another nine years. The last question, from an oak, is the best of the whole journey.

choices.text: Leave a teacher behind for the trees

effects.log: Namu, or an immortal like them, stays behind to keep answering. The forest is satisfied.

events.text: The travelling conference has come home to your terraces. The stone is set back in its place. Everything looks smaller and more beloved.

choices.text: Hold the next one at home, plainly

effects.log: A plain conference at home. Everyone talks about the journey and listens better for it.

choices.text: Promise to travel again in a thousand years

effects.log: The pantheons mark the date. They will hold you to it.

events.text: A minor god of markets has been selling front-row seats at your conference, which have always been free, for great sums of faith. The buyers are not pleased to learn they were free.

choices.text: Return the faith to the buyers

effects.log: You make the market god pay back every buyer. They do, slowly, and with bad grace.

choices.text: Make the market god attend a lecture

effects.log: The god of markets sits through a lecture on what cannot be bought. They come back the next cycle unpaid.
No more front rows. Everyone sits in a circle. The market god has nothing left to sell.

events.text: The god of markets has come back, without anything to sell, and sits on the lowest terrace taking notes on value. They ask if they may give a lecture on what things are worth.

effects.log: The market god lectures on worth. It is the most surprising lecture of the cycle, and almost tender.

choices.text: Ask them to ask a question instead

effects.log: They ask: "What is a lecture worth?" Nobody can answer. They seem satisfied.

events.text: A gifted young immortal argues before the conference that Cheon Uri's question has done harm: generations of students have wasted centuries on something that cannot be answered. They ask you to have it removed from the stone.
events.arc: The Student Who Would Erase the Question

effects.log: You hear it for a whole day. It is a good argument. You do not remove the question.
The conference votes. It is closer than you expected. The question stays, by nine voices.

choices.text: Ask them what they would carve instead

effects.log: They have an answer ready: their own question. It is a good question too.

events.text: The young immortal who wanted to erase the question has carved their own question on a stone at the foot of your terraces. Students have started to stop there first.
events.arc: The Student Who Would Erase the Question

effects.log: Two stones. Students stop at both. The young immortal comes up to yours, one day, and touches it.

choices.text: Bring it up beside the first

effects.log: You set their stone next to Cheon Uri's. The two questions argue for ever, side by side.

events.text: The young immortal who argued against the question, now old, admits to you that they have spent their whole life on it after all. They have not answered it. They are not sorry.
events.arc: The Student Who Would Erase the Question

effects.log: You laugh together on the stair for an hour.

choices.text: Add their name to Cheon Uri's list

effects.log: Cheon Uri, or their heir, adds the name to the list of those who said "I do not know."

events.text: Three other gods of heaven hold Dao conferences of their own, smaller, on other cycles. They write to propose a pact: no two conferences on the same years, and a shared Record of Questions.

effects.log: The Pact of Conferences is signed on your terrace. Heaven has a conference every few decades now.

choices.text: Agree to the dates, not the Record

effects.log: The dates are shared. Each keeps its own questions. Mok Hyeran, or their heir, is relieved.

events.text: One of the other hosts of the Pact of Conferences has died, or faded, or ascended; nobody is sure. Their students write to ask whether their conference should go on without a host.

choices.text: Tell them to host it themselves

effects.log: The students host it together, with no god at the front. It is very good.

choices.text: Offer to host it on their cycle

effects.log: You host two conferences now. You are very busy and very happy.

events.text: A wandering immortal musician, Kang Haeum, has begun playing a long flute on the stair during lectures, very softly. Some lecturers are furious. Some say they have never lectured better.

choices.text: Give them a place to play

effects.log: Kang Haeum plays from the edge of the high terrace. The lectures take on a rhythm.

choices.text: Ask them to play only between lectures

effects.log: The silence between lectures is filled with music. Students linger.

events.text: Kang Haeum has written music for Cheon Uri's question, a tune with no ending, that every immortal on the terraces can now hum. It has spread to heaven's markets.

effects.log: The conference opens with the tune with no ending. It is still going when the conference closes.

choices.text: Ask them to write an ending

effects.log: Kang Haeum tries for a century and fails. They are delighted to fail.

events.text: Kang Haeum has lost their flute in the clouds and cannot make another that sounds right. They sit on the stair, humming, and the whole terrace hums with them.

choices.text: Give them a flute from your own hall

effects.log: The flute is old and odd. In Kang Haeum's hands it sounds like the first night.

choices.text: Let the humming be the music

effects.log: The Humming Conference. Nobody ever forgets it.

events.text: A mortal child has climbed the pilgrim stair below as far as it goes, and then kept climbing, through cloud, by sheer stubbornness. They have appeared at your gate, frozen and exhausted, asking for the answer.

choices.text: Warm them and tell them the truth

effects.log: You wrap the child in your own robe and say you do not know. They cry, then laugh, then fall asleep.

choices.text: Give them a seat at the conference

effects.log: A mortal child sits in the front row of the Grand Dao Conference. The gods are very quiet around them.

events.text: The mortal child who climbed has gone home, below, and has grown, and is teaching the children of their town to climb, not the stair, but questions.

effects.log: A cup of the conference tea appears on their table one morning. They know exactly what it means.
You watch from above. The town below becomes known for its stubborn, curious children.

events.text: An old mortal climbs to the gate of your conference, through the cloud, by stubbornness, as they did once as a child. They want to ask one more time.

effects.log: They laugh. "Neither do I," they say. "I just wanted to say it to you." They go down content.

choices.text: Give them a better next birth

effects.log: You mark their next life: born somewhere a stair is easier. They will climb anyway.

events.text: Long after Kang Haeum has gone, the stair still hums a little in the evenings, when the wind comes from the Throne of Storms.

effects.log: You sit on the humming stair until dark.
The tune with no ending goes on in young mouths.

events.text: Between conferences the terraces are empty for decades. You walk them alone in the mornings and find small things left behind: a brush, a ribbon, a half-written question.

effects.log: You return every lost thing at the next conference. Some owners have forgotten they lost them.
The lost things wait. Their owners find them, and stand still a moment, remembering.

events.text: A terrace has cracked in a quake of the Throne of Storms. The masons say it will take a decade. You could mend it in a breath.

effects.log: The terrace is whole again. The masons are put out.

choices.text: Mend it with the masons, by hand

effects.log: You carry stones for a decade beside the masons. They tell you everything that is wrong with heaven.

events.text: You write the invitations to the next conference by hand, as you always have. This time there are twenty thousand. Your hand aches.

effects.log: Twenty thousand invitations, each in your hand. Some immortals keep theirs for a thousand years.
Your students write them. The handwriting is a riot. Nobody minds.

events.text: Between conferences the gardeners of heaven have planted the lowest terrace with herbs for the tea. It smells like rain and memory.

effects.log: You walk the herb terrace each morning. Your lectures grow gentler.

choices.text: Give it to the youngest students

effects.log: The youngest students tend the herbs and argue over weeds.

events.text: You find a box of letters from students who wrote to you between conferences, a thousand years of them, never answered because you thought you would answer at the next conference, and then forgot.

effects.log: You answer every letter. Many of the writers have ascended. Some write back.

choices.text: Read them, and answer at the next conference

effects.log: You read the oldest aloud at the opening. Some of the writers are there, mortified and moved.

events.text: Someone has put up a statue of you at the top of the great stair, very large and very solemn. It does not look like you at all. It is holding a book you have never read.

choices.text: Leave it, and hang a teacup on it

effects.log: The solemn statue holds a teacup now. It looks almost friendly.

choices.text: Ask for it to be taken down

effects.log: It is taken down. The stair is better without it.

events.text: A cat from somewhere has taken to sleeping on the stone of the first question in the afternoons. The Still Water says it is a teacher. The Open Hand says it is a cat.

effects.log: The cat sleeps on the question for twenty years. Nobody disturbs it.
The cat looks at you, and yawns, and goes back to sleep. The Still Water is triumphant.

events.text: A mortal scholar below has had a vision of your terraces and drawn a map of them. It is very nearly right. They have sent it up on a kite, with a question: "Is this where you are?"

effects.log: You add one stair to their map. They frame it below.

choices.text: Send a dream of the real terraces

effects.log: The scholar dreams them, and wakes, and draws a perfect map, and is happy.

events.text: You hear a lecture being given on an empty terrace at midnight. The voice is your own, from a conference long ago, caught somehow in the stone.

effects.log: Your young self was wrong in three places and right in one you had forgotten.
You answer your young self across the centuries. The stone goes quiet, satisfied.

events.text: A crane from the Green Assembly has dropped a feather on your desk. It writes by itself, if you hold it lightly. It writes only questions.

choices.text: Use it to write the invitations

effects.log: Every invitation to the next conference is a question. Attendance doubles.

choices.text: Give it to Mok Hyeran's Record

effects.log: The feather lives in the Record, writing questions in the night.

events.text: You find Noegong of the Nine Drums rehearsing quietly on the empty terraces between conferences, so as to drum better at the next one. They are embarrassed to be seen.

effects.log: You listen to the god of Thunder practise. They play better with an audience.
You go round by the other stair. At the next conference the drumming is perfect.

events.text: A student tells you, red-faced, that they dreamt you were their student and they had to teach you everything, and you were very slow.

effects.log: They tell you. It is a good lesson. You were very slow, they say, but you tried.

choices.text: Promise to be a better student

effects.log: They laugh, and then look at you, and see you mean it.

events.text: The calligraphers of heaven have asked you to write Cheon Uri's question in a single stroke, for a scroll to hang in the Heavenly Court.

ok.log: One stroke. The question hangs in the Court, and officials stop in front of it.

fail.log: The stroke breaks halfway. You hang the broken one. It is more honest.

choices.text: Write it slowly, in many strokes

effects.log: A careful, many-stroked question hangs in the Court. It is very clear.

events.text: A hero you sent down to {sov_world} as the best student of a conference has returned for a visit. They have grown old in your Pocket World and taught a whole people to ask.

effects.log: They sit by the stone and tell the conference about {sov_world}. The gods are very quiet.

choices.text: Ask them what the people ask

effects.log: They tell you. {sov_world} asks mostly about you. You are humbled.

events.text: In {sov_world} it has not rained for a year. The people there have stopped asking questions and started praying. It is a different sound, coming up.

choices.text: Send rain, and a question with it

effects.log: Rain falls on {sov_world}, and in every drop a question. The people laugh in the rain.

choices.text: Send a teacher instead of rain

effects.log: A student goes down and teaches them to find water. The rain comes later, and they are ready.

events.text: The Heavenly Calendar has lost a day, somehow, and your conference is now a day earlier than everyone thinks. Ten thousand immortals will arrive tomorrow to find it half over.

effects.log: Everybody gets a first day. The Calendar keepers are grateful.
You begin to an empty terrace and repeat it all next day. It is better the second time.

events.text: The youngest herald of the conference has asked to learn to lecture, instead of announcing lectures. They have been listening from the doorway for three hundred years.

effects.log: The herald lectures on doorways and listening. It is wonderful.
You teach the herald privately for a century. They become a quiet, fine teacher.

events.text: Your oldest robe, the one you wore on the first night, has worn through at the elbow. A student offers to mend it. Another says it should be kept as it is.

effects.log: The robe is mended with thread from every terrace. You wear it at the opening.
The torn robe hangs by the stone. Students touch the elbow for luck.

events.text: A god of a small river has come to ask whether a river is the water or the bed. Their river has changed its course and they do not know if they are still its god.

effects.log: The river god thinks about it, and goes home to their new course, comforted.
The Keeper of Tides takes them to the sea and shows them where every river ends.

events.text: You have broken, in your long life of hosting, two hundred teacups. Someone has kept every shard. They have made a mosaic of them on the floor of the high terrace.

effects.log: It is smooth and cool. You know every cup.
You break a cup on purpose and give them the shards. The mosaic grows.

events.text: A rumour has gone round heaven that you mean to stop hosting the conference. Nobody knows where it began. Students have started arriving early to make sure of their seats while they can.

effects.log: You deny it from the high terrace. The students cheer, and stay early anyway.

choices.text: Ask yourself if it is true

effects.log: You think about it for a decade. It is not true yet.

events.text: Young immortals have begun to whisper wishes to the stone of the first question, as if it were a well. You overheard one: they wished to be asked a question nobody else could answer.

effects.log: You ask the young immortal a question only they could answer. They answer it, astonished.
The stone keeps it. Years later, someone does ask them. It changes their life.

events.text: A tremor runs through heaven during a lecture. Cups rattle, stairs creak. Ten thousand immortals look at you to see if they should be afraid.

effects.log: You go on. The tremor passes. Afterwards students say that was the lesson.
You stop and listen to heaven shake. It is, somehow, the most beautiful sound of the conference.

events.text: At the end of every conference day you drink one last cup on the high terrace, alone, looking out over the clouds. Today there is someone already there, in your place, drinking from your cup.

effects.log: It is a stranger. You drink together. You never learn their name. It is one of your best evenings.
You bring another cup and sit a little apart. At the end, they nod to you and go.

events.text: A tyrant below the clouds has burned every copy of your sayings in their realm. Mortals are learning them by heart instead, and reciting them in secret.

choices.text: Send them a dream of the conference

effects.log: Every reciter below dreams of your terraces. They wake braver.
The tyrant falls in a generation. The sayings do not.

events.text: The children of gods play a game on your terraces between conferences: one is the god on the stone, and the others ask questions, and whoever can answer becomes the god. Nobody ever wins.

effects.log: You play the questioner. A small god answers you, and wins, the first ever. Everyone is furious and delighted.
You watch the game until dark. It is the best conference you have seen in years.

events.text: You have decided, for once, to lecture at dawn, before anyone is awake. Only the heralds, Bang Soyul's kettle and a few sleepless immortals hear it.

effects.log: The few remember the dawn lecture all their lives.
You speak to the sun coming up. The gods of the Will of Heaven say they heard it in their halls.

events.text: Two immortals who have never met, from opposite ends of heaven, have given the same answer to the same hard question at your conference, word for word. Each accuses the other of copying.

effects.log: They sit together and find they had the same teacher below, ages ago, in different lives.

choices.text: Declare it a sign the answer is true

effects.log: The answer is honoured. The two immortals remain suspicious of each other for a century.

events.text: The two immortals who answered alike have gone looking for their shared teacher below. They have found a mortal schoolroom, very old, and an old teacher who does not remember either of them.

choices.text: Let them teach in that schoolroom

effects.log: The two immortals teach below for a decade. The old teacher sits at the back, pleased.

choices.text: Bring the old teacher up to the conference

effects.log: A mortal teacher sits on your terrace, bewildered, while two immortals bow to them.

events.text: A god of a stern domain, who has never once been unsure in ten thousand years, has caught doubt at your conference like a cold. They are horrified. Their worshippers can feel it.
events.arc: The God Who Learned to Doubt

effects.log: It passes. The god is relieved, and slightly sorry.

choices.text: Tell them it is a gift

effects.log: They do not believe you. They keep the doubt anyway, carefully, like a seed.

events.text: The god who caught doubt at your conference has begun to answer their worshippers' prayers more slowly, and more kindly. Their temples below report fewer miracles and more consolation.
events.arc: The God Who Learned to Doubt

effects.log: "Heavier," they say. "And better." They stay for the closing lecture for the first time.
You send a dream below. The worshippers say their god seems to listen now.

events.text: A god who walks the Calamity Star's path, raiding domains and isles, has sent one of their own lieutenants to your conference in disguise. The lieutenant is found out on the first day, and the terraces are in uproar.

effects.log: The lieutenant stays, and sits alone, and listens to every word with a strange hunger.

choices.text: Send them back with a question

effects.log: You send the lieutenant home with a question for their master: "What do you keep?"
The lieutenant leaves without a fight. They look back once from the stair.

events.text: The lieutenant of the Calamity Star has left their master's host and come back to your gate, alone and unarmed, asking to learn. They have done things they will not speak of.

effects.log: They become a student. They never speak of the raids. They are the gentlest teacher of the young you ever have.

choices.text: Send them to make amends first

effects.log: They go to every isle they raided. It takes two centuries. Then they come back.

events.text: The bell-founders of the Throne of Storms have finally cast a new bell for the conference. It is enormous. When they ring it to test it, three clouds fall out of the sky.

effects.log: The giant bell hangs over the terraces. Its first opening is heard in the mortal world below.
The founders, offended, cast a bell the size of a teacup. It rings perfectly.

events.text: Mortals below the clouds have heard the new bell of the conference ring, once every few decades, and built a festival around it. They believe it means the gods are learning.

effects.log: They are right. The festival grows. Faith of a cheerful kind rises from below.

choices.text: Send them a lecture with the next ring

effects.log: With the next ring, every mortal below hears one sentence. They argue about it for a generation.

events.text: Two gods are about to go to war over a border of clouds. Both of them attend your conference. Both arrive with their generals. The terraces feel like a powder store.
events.arc: The War That Was a Question

effects.log: You seat the two gods side by side for a lecture. They do not look at each other for three days.
You lecture on borders. Both gods take it personally. Both are moved.

choices.text: Ask them each one question, privately

ok.log: You ask each what they would lose. Their answers are the same. They go home and do not fight.

fail.log: Neither will answer. They leave early.

events.text: The two gods who almost went to war over a border of clouds have decided to share it. They have asked you to name it, since it was settled at your conference.
events.arc: The War That Was a Question

effects.log: The Asked Border is the most peaceful edge in heaven.
They argue about the name for a century. It is a much better argument than a war.

events.text: An old immortal, Seol Bom, has attended your conference for two thousand years and has, this cycle, forgotten why they come. They are not upset. They are curious.

effects.log: You find their first question in the Record. They read it and laugh: it was about whether gods eat.

choices.text: Help them find a new reason

effects.log: Seol Bom decides they come for the tea. It is a perfectly good reason.

events.text: Seol Bom, who forgot why they come, now comes for a new reason every cycle: once for the tea, once for the bell, once for a particular cloud. They say it keeps them young.

choices.text: Ask what this cycle's reason is

effects.log: "You," they say, and pat your hand, and go to their seat.
You start choosing a reason each cycle too. Your conferences grow lighter.

events.text: A raider of the Calamity Star's kind, wounded, has crawled to the gate of your conference and asked for sanctuary. Gods who lost domains to such raiders are sitting in your front row.

effects.log: You give it. The front row is furious. The raider heals, and leaves, and does not raid again.

choices.text: Heal them and send them on

effects.log: You heal them at the gate and send them away before the front row sees.

events.text: The gods of the Asked Border send you a gift every century: a cloud from their shared border, folded small, with tea leaves inside it.

effects.log: Cloud tea, at the opening. It tastes of peace, a little thin.

choices.text: Send back a cup of yours

effects.log: A cup goes back across heaven to the Asked Border.

events.text: A young god tells you that their teacher's teacher was at the first conference, and that the thing they still repeat about it is not the question but your answer: "I do not know."

effects.log: You say it again. The young god looks as if they have been given something heavy and precious.

choices.text: Tell them what you wish you had said

effects.log: You tell them. They say they prefer the first one.

events.text: Your clever answer from the first night, the one Cheon Uri wrote under a question mark, has become a saying in heaven. You hear it quoted at a market of the gods, slightly wrong, by someone selling fans.

effects.log: You correct the fan-seller. They are delighted to meet the source and sell you a fan.
The wrong version is better, you decide. You walk on, smiling.

events.text: Immortals who cannot come to your conference have begun to carve Cheon Uri's question on stones in their own halls, as you carved it on the first night. There are said to be a thousand such stones in heaven.

effects.log: You find one in a small hall far away, worn smooth by a single immortal's hand. You sit with them.

choices.text: Ask Mok Hyeran to list them

effects.log: The Record lists every stone. You read the list like a map of heaven's doubts.

events.text: Students of the Still Water, the school you once sat with, have begun to sit in your front row in silence and not take notes. Other lecturers find it unnerving.

effects.log: You teach to the silent row. You find yourself saying less, and better.

choices.text: Ask one of them to speak

effects.log: One speaks: a single sentence. It is the best thing said at the conference.

events.text: Students of the Open Hand, the school you once walked out with, have begun bringing mortals to the conference as their guests. The mortals are terrified and fascinated.

effects.log: You greet every mortal guest by the gate. They go down below with stories.

choices.text: Give them a terrace of their own

effects.log: The mortal guests have a terrace. Some gods sneak in to listen.

events.text: The teapot you set between the two schools on one terrace long ago has become a relic. Students of both schools take turns polishing it. It is very shiny and never used.

effects.log: You brew tea in the relic. Both schools are scandalised, and drink it.
It shines on the terrace. The two schools polish it in turns, and talk while they polish.

events.text: Teachers all over heaven have begun to bow to their students when the students surpass them. They say they learned it from you. Some of them do it rather too often.

effects.log: You bow to a student who has done nothing remarkable. They are confused, then very proud.
A short lecture. Teachers bow less often, and mean it more.

events.text: A student you corrected publicly long ago has a student of their own now, and you hear them correct that student publicly, gently, in exactly your words.

effects.log: You tell them how it felt to be corrected. They had never thought of it. They teach differently after.

choices.text: Let them find their own way

effects.log: You say nothing. Years later they correct someone privately, and you smile.

events.text: You still have the notes you took that night at your student's feet. You read them now and find, in the margin, a question you wrote then and never answered.

effects.log: It takes you a week. The answer is something you could not have known then.
Your old student reads it and laughs. "I wondered when you would ask," they say.

events.text: Do Yeonhwa, or the clerk who came after, tells you that the page cut from the Book of Fates has been seen again: it appears, now and then, between other pages, blank line and all.

choices.text: Ask them to leave it when it comes

effects.log: The clerks leave it when it comes. It comes more often.
You see it, once, between two ordinary fates. The blank line seems to wait for you.

events.text: Your seal on the blank page of the Book of Fates has become famous among the clerks. They have nicknamed it the Supreme's Mercy, and they touch it for luck on hard days.

choices.text: Tell them it was not mercy

effects.log: You tell them it was curiosity. They like it even more.
Two seals on the blank page now. The clerks are thrilled.

events.text: The single word you wrote under the question in the Book of Fates has begun, very slowly, to change its spelling. Do Yeonhwa says words in the Book do that when they are still alive.

effects.log: The word grows. You do not look at it for a thousand years.

ok.log: It has become two words. The second one is not yours. You are glad.

fail.log: You cannot read it now. It is no longer only yours.

events.text: The Third Terrace, for asking together, has become so crowded that the circles of immortals overlap, and nobody is sure which conversation they are in.

effects.log: You build another. It fills too. Heaven is talking.
Overlapping circles. Questions cross from one to another. Some of the best answers come from the crossings.

events.text: Since your dream of the pieces, you sometimes see, out of the corner of your eye, every immortal at the conference holding a small light. When you look directly, it is gone.

effects.log: You lecture from the corner of your eye. The lights stay.
They do not believe you. Then one of them sees it too.

events.text: Sitting in your student's conference as a guest became, for you, a custom. Their heralds now keep a front seat empty with your name on a small card. Today someone has sat in it by mistake.

effects.log: You sit beside the stranger in the second seat. They never know.
You sit in the back. Your student sees, and smiles, and teaches to the back row.

events.text: The century of the clashing conferences is remembered in heaven as the Year of Two Stones. Immortals who attended both still argue about which was better. You overhear one argument.

effects.log: You say your student's was better. The arguers fall silent in awe.
Nobody believes you. Everybody agrees.

events.text: The student whose flaw you named and who mended it now teaches mending: how to find the flaw in your own understanding and close it without shame.

effects.log: You attend. You find a flaw of your own. You mend it, without shame, in front of them.
They mend twelve hard students in a century.

events.text: Cheon Uri has written "Still no" on the first page of every book they keep, as a reminder. They show you the newest book. The first page says, in your handwriting, borrowed: "Still no."

effects.log: You write it again under their copy. It looks right twice.
You add two words. Cheon Uri reads them and is quiet for a long time.

events.text: Cheon Uri has told no one the word you whispered to them. They tell you that every year they are tempted. Every year they decide the question is better without it.

effects.log: They think about it, and keep it anyway.
They nod. "I thought so," they say.

events.text: Cheon Uri's book of every answer is now read aloud, page by page, at the opening of each conference. It will take ten thousand years to finish. Nobody is in a hurry.

effects.log: You read today's page. It is an answer by a child, about clouds.

choices.text: Add an answer of your own

effects.log: You add one at the back. Someone will read it aloud in ten thousand years.

events.text: Since the year of silence, every conference has begun with one minute in which nobody speaks. A child of a god laughing ends it, if one is present. Parents bring children for the purpose.

effects.log: The minute of silence and the child's laugh open every conference after.
You laugh to end the silence. Everyone is astonished. Then they laugh.

events.text: Cheon Uri, keeper of the stone, reads the question at every opening now. Their voice shakes less each time. This time it does not shake at all, and they look up at you, surprised.

effects.log: You nod. They nod back. Something passes between you that is not a word.
You applaud. The whole conference applauds the keeper. Cheon Uri hides their face.

events.text: The child who reads the question at the opening has grown up. They read it now with a grown voice, and the old immortals who wept the first time weep again, for different reasons.

effects.log: They read for another thousand years.
A new child reads it, stumbling. The grown keeper stands behind them.

events.text: The student who outgrew you, now keeper of the reading, has changed one word of how they read it. Only you notice. It is a better word.

effects.log: They blush. They had been afraid you would mind.

choices.text: Say nothing, and use it too

effects.log: You use the new word from then on. So does heaven.

events.text: Mortals below have built a shrine with no statue in it, only an empty seat and a stone with a question carved on it. They do not know whose it is. The priests of three gods are claiming it.

effects.log: You send a dream: the shrine belongs to whoever asks there. The three priests are annoyed and then curious.
You sit in the empty seat for an hour. A mortal comes in, asks a question aloud, and leaves without waiting.

events.text: The shrine of questions below has a keeper now: a mortal who listens to every question asked there and writes none of them down, by rule. They are very old. They have asked, in a prayer, who will listen after them.

choices.text: Send them a successor in a dream

effects.log: A young mortal dreams of the empty seat. They come to the shrine the next morning.
You promise. From then on, a little of you is always in the empty seat below.

events.text: One of your students, Pyo Hyesung, has been cast down from heaven by the Heavenly Court for breaking a law of the domains in anger. They write from the Upper Realm below: they deserved it, they say, and they would like to keep studying.

effects.log: Every conference, a copy of your lectures goes down to Pyo Hyesung. They study in a cave.
The Court shortens the sentence by a third. Pyo Hyesung writes that they did not ask you to.

events.text: Pyo Hyesung has climbed back up to heaven at the end of their sentence, on their own, the long way. They stand at your gate in a worn robe and ask if their old seat is still theirs.

effects.log: They sit. The student beside them, who arrived after the fall, moves over without being asked.

choices.text: Ask them to lecture on falling

effects.log: Pyo Hyesung lectures on falling and climbing. It is the most useful lecture of the century.

events.text: An apprentice oracle of the Silent Hall has run away to your conference. They can see the future of anyone who asks them a question, and they want to learn how not to.
events.arc: The Oracle Who Would Not Foresee

choices.text: Teach them to listen without seeing

effects.log: It takes a century. They learn to hear a question as a question.

choices.text: Send them back to the Silent Hall

effects.log: They go back. Mongsa the Sleeper writes to thank you; the Hall had been worried.

events.text: The apprentice oracle who learned not to foresee has seen something anyway, by accident: one moment of your own future. They will not say what. They are smiling.
events.arc: The Oracle Who Would Not Foresee

effects.log: You do not ask. You think about their smile on hard days.

ok.log: You guess right. They laugh so hard they cannot stand.

fail.log: You guess wrong. They laugh anyway.

events.text: Young immortals of your conference have invented a hunt: they go out across heaven to find questions nobody has asked yet, and bring them back like game.

effects.log: You judge the catch at the closing. The winning question is from a god of puddles.
You go out with them and come back with nothing. They are kind about it.

events.text: A mortal below, looking up at the right moment, has seen the edge of your terraces through a break in the cloud, and fallen to their knees in a field.

effects.log: The cloud closes. The mortal tells the story all their life and is never believed. They do not mind.
You wave. They wave back, astonished. It becomes a story in their family for a hundred years.

events.text: You visit a school of yours on a far edge of heaven, founded by a student of a student of a student. Nobody there recognises you. They are teaching your first lecture, slightly wrong.

effects.log: You sit in the back. It is a good lecture, wrong in an interesting way.
The school is overwhelmed. You spend a week being polite. You would rather have sat in the back.

events.text: A student has burned all their notes from your conference, in grief, after their teacher faded. They come to you with the ashes in a bowl.

effects.log: You bury the ashes by the stone. The student comes to the place every cycle.
You teach them every lecture again, privately, over a century. It is slower and better.

events.text: An immortal asks you to help them unlearn something you taught them, which has become a wall in their mind.

ok.log: You lift the old teaching out of their mind. There is room there now.

fail.log: It will not come out. You teach them a door in it instead.

effects.log: They hold both, and the wall becomes a gate.

events.text: There is a room at the back of your hall you sealed thousands of years ago and have forgotten why. Your students have found it.

effects.log: Inside is your first lecture, unfinished, and a cup of tea, long dry. You finish the lecture.
You must have had a reason. You trust your younger self, for once.

events.text: Cheonho, Who Hangs the Stars, has hung a new constellation in your honour: one bright star and ten thousand faint ones around it. They tell you, kindly, that the bright one is not you.

effects.log: "The question," says Cheonho. You laugh with delight.

choices.text: Find yourself among the faint ones

effects.log: You find yourself, at last, somewhere in the middle. It feels right.

events.text: You dream of pouring tea for a stranger on the high terrace, who drinks and says, "You have not changed." You wake not knowing whether it was praise.

effects.log: You decide it was. You lecture well that cycle.
You change three things in your teaching. They are good changes.

events.text: At every shrine of yours below, mortals have begun to leave a cup of water rather than incense, because a story says you prefer it. You do.

effects.log: Water left at your shrines is good water. Mortals below drink it, and ask better questions for a day.

choices.text: Send the story a little further

effects.log: The story spreads. So do the cups.

events.text: A young god trembles at the sight of you on the stair, and you realise, with a shock, that you are one of the oldest and most powerful things in heaven now.

choices.text: Sit on the stair so you are lower

effects.log: You sit. The young god sits too. You talk about the weather. They stop trembling.

choices.text: Ask them to show you their domain

effects.log: They show you a domain of dew on spiderwebs. You are enchanted. They forget to be afraid.

events.text: You visit a mortal schoolroom below in plain clothes. The teacher is explaining that the gods know everything. A child at the back is frowning.

effects.log: The child grins. Years later they climb the clouds to find out why.
You leave. The child keeps frowning. That is enough.

events.text: A star that Ha Jiwoo once hung has gone out. Ha Jiwoo is inconsolable. Cheonho says stars go out; it is what they do.

choices.text: Sit with Ha Jiwoo under the dark place

effects.log: You sit with them where the star was. Another star, faint and new, appears nearby.

choices.text: Help them hang a new one

effects.log: You hang a new star together, also crooked.

events.text: The first teacup of the conference has gone missing. Students search the terraces for a week. It is found at last in Namu's roots, held very gently.

effects.log: The tree keeps the cup. Nobody argues with a tree.

choices.text: Take it back, and thank the tree

effects.log: You thank Namu and take the cup. A leaf falls on your head.

events.text: An oracle comes to ask if you would like to know when your last conference will be. They are very gentle about it.

effects.log: You decline. Every conference is the last one, you think, and the first.

choices.text: Ask them instead what they would like to learn

effects.log: The oracle is startled. They stay for the conference, as a student.

events.text: A god of the unmaking has come to the conference and asked, quite politely, whether a question can be unmade. They would like to try it on Cheon Uri's.

effects.log: They try for a week. The question is still there. The god is delighted: it is the first thing they could not unmake.

choices.text: Ask them what they would unmake instead

effects.log: They think about it. "My own fear," they say. You help.

events.text: A temple of yours below that burned long ago has been rebuilt by the grandchildren of the people who burned it, who are ashamed. They have left the scorched lintel in place over the door.

effects.log: You bless the temple and the lintel and the grandchildren. Faith rises like warm smoke.

choices.text: Send a question to be carved under the lintel

effects.log: Under the scorched lintel the grandchildren carve: "Who are you waiting for?"

events.text: You visit an old rival's empty hall, long after they have ascended or faded, and find your own lectures on their shelf, heavily annotated, in their hand, with many exclamation marks.

effects.log: Half are furious. Half are delighted. All are about you.
You write in the margin: "You were right here." Someone will find it.

events.text: Your very first student at the Grand Dao Conference, Oh Gyeol, who sat in the front row on the first night, has returned after thousands of years away beyond heaven. They look younger than you. They bring a gift wrapped in cloud.

effects.log: Inside is a cup from beyond heaven. The tea it makes tastes of the first night.
They tell you of conferences beyond heaven, where the gods ask the same question in other words.

events.text: Oh Gyeol, your first student, has asked to sit in the front row once more, in the same place as on the first night. A young immortal is sitting there and does not know who they are.

choices.text: Seat them beside the young one

effects.log: First student and newest student side by side. The young one asks Oh Gyeol something, and they answer, kindly.
Oh Gyeol sits in the back row. "The front is for the beginning," they say.

events.text: Oh Gyeol is leaving again, for beyond heaven. At the gate they ask if you have a message for the conferences out there, where the gods ask the same question.

choices.text: "Tell them we do not know either."

effects.log: Oh Gyeol laughs. "They will be so relieved," they say, and go.

choices.text: Send them with a stone from your terrace

effects.log: A stone from your terraces goes beyond heaven, carved with Cheon Uri's question.

events.text: You have decided, privately, to take one last personal student, after all the thousands. The terraces do not know. You watch the new immortals for a whole conference, choosing.

choices.text: Choose the one who asks most

effects.log: A loud young immortal who never stops asking. They are exhausting. You are very happy.

choices.text: Choose the one who asks least

effects.log: A silent young immortal in the back. When they finally ask something, it is enormous.
You leave it to chance. The one who touches the stone first the next morning is a cook.

events.text: Your last student has learned everything you can teach in a century, and now stands before you asking what is left. Nothing is left. You have been dreading this.

effects.log: They teach you, for a decade. You learn things about yourself you had not known.
They go. You watch them down the great stair, and it is the hardest and best thing you have done in a thousand years.

events.text: You have begun writing a last lecture, for whenever it is needed. You have rewritten it ninety times. Each version is shorter.

effects.log: The ninety-first version is one line. You think it may be finished.
You throw it away. When the time comes, you will know what to say.

events.text: You look yourself up in the Record of Questions and find hundreds of thousands of entries under your name: every question you ever asked aloud at the conference.

effects.log: They are clumsy and brave. You wish you could tell your younger self so.
They are short. Most of them are "Why?" You are pleased.

events.text: You make the conference tea alone at dawn in the empty kitchen, as you have done ten thousand times, and for the first time it comes out perfectly, and nobody is there to taste it.

effects.log: It is perfect. You laugh aloud in the empty kitchen.
You pour the perfect tea over the stone of the first question. It runs into every letter.

events.text: Your students have drawn a chart of every teacher who learned from you, and every teacher who learned from them. It covers a wall of the high terrace, and then the next wall.

effects.log: At the very edge is a mortal schoolteacher below who has never heard your name.
"It does not end," you say. They stop, and leave the edge blank, on purpose.

events.text: For the first time in all the ages, you are late to your own opening. When you arrive, breathless, the conference has started without you, and is going very well.

choices.text: Sit in the back and listen

effects.log: You sit in the back of your own conference. It is wonderful.
You apologise and take over. The students are a little disappointed.

events.text: Lightning strikes the stone of the first question during a storm of the Throne of Storms. When the smoke clears, the carved question glows faintly, and goes on glowing for a year.

choices.text: Hold night lectures by its light

effects.log: A year of lectures by the light of the question. Students say they thought more clearly.
The god of Thunder insists it was not them. Nobody believes it. They are pleased anyway.

events.text: The clouds around your terraces have arranged themselves, this morning, into the shape of a question mark. The gods of the Throne of Storms say they had nothing to do with it.

effects.log: You bow to the clouds. They drift apart, satisfied.
A lecture on the question mark. It is short and happy.

events.text: Someone has counted, and this conference you have poured your thousandth thousand cup of tea. The heralds want to mark it. You do not remember any of the cups in particular. You remember all of them.

choices.text: Pour the next one as usual

effects.log: You pour the next one as if it were the first. It is.
A student pours the millionth and first. Their hand shakes.

events.text: {sov_heir} and {sov_strival} have met on the great stair, the one who carries your Dao and the one who turned against it. Both look up at you on the terrace, waiting to see if you will come down.

choices.text: Come down and stand between them

effects.log: You stand between them on the stair. After a while all three of you are talking about tea.
They talk without you. When they come up, they are arguing pleasantly.

events.text: {sov_student} has written you a letter, though you see them every cycle. It says only what they never managed to say aloud. It is very short.

effects.log: You write back, just as short. Neither of you ever mentions the letters.
You say it aloud on the stair. {sov_student} goes very red and very still.

events.text: You notice that, at every conference, there is one seat on the lowest terrace that is always empty, though the terraces are full. Nobody has ever sat there. Nobody can say why.

effects.log: From the lowest seat the stone looks very far away and very bright. You understand your students better.
It stays empty. You decide it is for whoever is coming next.

events.text: Before dawn on the opening day, {sov_heir} is already sweeping the stair, as Yeon Seorin taught, though they never met Yeon Seorin. You pick up a second broom.

effects.log: You sweep the whole stair together. The sun comes up. It is enough.
"You did," they say, "by doing it." You had not known you were seen.

events.text: At the closing of this conference, without anyone arranging it, ten thousand immortals stand and bow to you at once. You have never seen it before. You do not know what to do with your hands.

effects.log: You bow lower. They bow lower. It goes on until someone laughs.
You turn to the kettle. It is the only answer you have. It is the right one.

events.text: Mortals below have begun to brew a tea they call the Supreme's Cup, leaves first, water too hot, wait too long. It is very bad tea. They drink it at the start of every lesson.

effects.log: The bad tea of the world below is blessed. It stays bad, and lessons begin well.

choices.text: Send them the secret of waiting

effects.log: You send a dream of waiting a little longer. Their tea improves. So do their lessons.

events.text: A student asks you, in front of everyone, what you are afraid of. The terraces go quiet. Nobody has ever asked you that aloud.

effects.log: You tell them: that one day nobody will climb the stair. They nod. They will climb it, they say.
They are afraid of being ordinary. You talk about that instead, for a long time.

events.text: A student of the Dao of Space has drawn a map of the conference in which every terrace is placed not where it is but where its questions lead. The stone of the first question is at the centre, and also at every edge.

effects.log: The map hangs in the hall. Students get lost in it happily.

choices.text: Ask where you are on it

effects.log: You are not on it. "You are the paper," the student says.

events.text: The plain iron sword over the conference gate, Gwak Taeseong's first, has begun to rust. The sword immortals want to polish it. The Still Water says rust is honest.

effects.log: It rusts, slowly, over the gate. Sword immortals bow to it more, not less.
You polish it once, by hand. It shines dully, like a memory.

events.text: The children of gods from all four pantheons have formed a class of their own on the lowest terrace, and refuse to sit with their parents' pantheons. They want a teacher who belongs to none.

effects.log: You teach the children of four pantheons together. They argue about everything except you.
Cheon Uri, a child of a god nobody remembers, is perfect for them.

events.text: Immortals born mortal now outnumber the heaven-born at your conference for the first time. Some old gods have noticed and do not like it.

choices.text: Lecture on where everyone was born

effects.log: You lecture on beginnings. The old gods leave in a huff, and come back the next day.

choices.text: Say nothing; let them sit together

effects.log: The mortal-born and the heaven-born sit together. Within a century nobody counts.

events.text: The great kettle of the conference has begun to sing when it boils, a long note that sounds like the start of a lecture. Students now wait for it before they sit.

choices.text: Begin every lecture on its note

effects.log: The kettle starts every lecture. It is a better opening than any bell.
Nobody did. It learned, the tea-keepers say, from listening.

events.text: Every immortal who has ever left your conference for good has written a letter on their way out. Someone has kept them all. There are more letters than there were students.

effects.log: Some wrote twice. Some wrote for friends who could not. One wrote for a tree.
It says: "Thank you for not knowing." You put it back very carefully.

events.text: The Concord of Domains has asked you to open its next session with a lecture, any lecture, so that the gods arrive in a listening mood.

effects.log: The gods of the twelve domains listen to a lecture on listening. The session is the shortest on record.
You pour for twelve gods in silence. They settle two quarrels before the cups are empty.

events.text: A mortal child below prays to you every night, not for anything, but to tell you one thing they wondered about that day. Tonight it is whether stars are lonely.

effects.log: Cheonho, Who Hangs the Stars, sends the child a dream of every star waving.
You wonder it too, all night. In the morning you lecture on it.

events.text: A new immortal has counted the stairs to your conference and found one more than everyone else counts. They count again and again. Always one more.

choices.text: Tell them it is the one they bring

effects.log: They think about it all the way up. At the top they are smiling.
You count together. You get the usual number. They get one more. Both are right.

events.text: The Heavenly Court, as a body, has sent a question to your conference for the first time ever. It is very formally worded and amounts to: "Are we doing well?"

effects.log: Your answer is read aloud before the whole Court. Several judges remove their hats.

choices.text: Invite the Court to ask it in person

effects.log: Three judges come, nervous, and ask it from the third row. The terraces answer them.

events.text: A god who came to your conference as a child of a pantheon now leads that pantheon. They come back and sit, by choice, on the lowest terrace, where the children sit.

effects.log: Two very old friends on the lowest terrace, among children.

choices.text: Ask them to teach the children

effects.log: The pantheon's leader teaches the children. It is the gentlest thing that pantheon has done in an age.

events.text: You keep watch one night on the high terrace, as you sometimes do, and count the lights of the immortals walking home along the golden roads after the conference. They go out one by one, very slowly.

effects.log: The last light goes out near dawn. You go to bed full.
You light a lamp at the top of the stair. Far off, someone turns and waves.

events.text: At the end of the conference, a student asks you to close it, for once, with a question instead of a lecture.

effects.log: You close with the first question. The terraces answer it with silence, which is the right answer.
You close with a question nobody has heard. Ten thousand immortals walk home thinking.
